supplementary_news.content: Health Matters Weekdays · The latest health news and expert advice on living well. Thank you for signing up! Hepatitis B can be a silent killer. It can pass from mother to child during birth and can spread through contact with infected blood or semen. Among babies infected before they turn 1, up to 90% develop a chronic, potentially lifelong infection, for which there are treatments but no cure. People may not even know they have the virus until their liver fails or they develop cancer, years later. Early-in-life hepatitis B infections, left untreated, lead to a 1 in 4 lifetime chance of developing liver cancer. In the U.S., hepatitis B vaccination became routinely recommended for all infants in 1991; later guidance specified that the first dose should happen within 24 hours of birth. However, in Dec. 2025, the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) under the Trump Administration moved to cease recommending this practice for babies born to mothers who test negative, instead advising a shared decision-making model where parents and clinicians decide together what is medically appropriate: a dose shortly after birth, or a first dose "no earlier than 2 months of age." (For babies born to mothers who test positive or whose status is unknown, the CDC continues to recommend a dose shortly after birth.) A new study, published today in Annals of Internal Medicine, uses computer modeling to simulate the hepatitis B infection status of an entire year’s worth of children born in the U.S. under the new recommendations over their first 20 years of life. The researchers find that if only about 26% of children are vaccinated—an estimate of what would occur under shared decision-making—chronic hepatitis B cases would rise by 225%. When should kids get the first dose of hepatitis B vaccine? The American Association of Pediatrics continues to recommend vaccination at birth against hepatitis B for all infants, and 15 states have sued the Trump Administration over vaccination schedule changes. “It's been challenged in many states and by professional societies, but we wanted to add some evidence to the conversation about what the potential impact of those changes could be,” says Dr. Amir Mohareb, an infectious-disease researcher at Harvard Medical School and Massachusetts General Hospital who is an author of the new study. The simulation modeled how many of 3.6 million children, born the same year in the U.S., would develop hepatitis B under a number of scenarios, including if the former CDC recommendations continued to be followed, if the initial dose (also called a “birth dose”) was delayed, and if a shared decision-making scenario was employed. The model suggests that if the first dose is delayed until 2 months old, and only 75% of infants get it, then there would be a 19% increase in chronic cases compared to if every child received their first dose at birth. With a 26% vaccination rate at 2 months, the number climbed to 225%. This study modeled only at a single year of births, notes Mahoreb. “Imagine that happening year after year after year after year. That could quickly become thousands and thousands of new infections, and even a small number of new infections could result in lifelong chronic infection that could be detrimental to families, lead to more cases of cancer, and [become] costly to the health care system,” Mohareb says. Two other recent modeling studies have looked at the impacts of changing hepatitis B vaccine recommendations. One found that if vaccination no longer occurred at birth, a substantial increase in screening pregnant women for the virus would be necessary to keep infection numbers in infants down. Another, looking at the economic ramifications, found that even if every child eventually received the vaccine, delaying the first dose by 2 months yielded an additional $16.4 million in health care spending on new infections. “All three of these studies complement each other, in a good way, and provide some modicum of evidence so that we don't need to risk doing a clinical trial or testing this on people,” Mahoreb says. “We have done those experiments.” Decades ago, he continues, clinical trials already proved the efficacy of the existing approach, “so that we would have the benefit now of advancing medical progress and not needing to reopen that question.”

Infectious Disease > Hepatitis Study Warns of More Chronic Hepatitis B in the Years Ahead — Shift to shared decision-making for vaccine recommendation would up chronic infections by 83% by Terrence Rudd, Staff Writer, MedPage Today October 19, 2026 • 3 min read Add MedPage Today on Google MedpageToday Key Takeaways The CDC's Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices abandoned more than three decades of U.S. vaccine policy and voted to stop recommending a universal birth dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. Choosing shared clinical decision-making instead of a birth dose could increase chronic hepatitis B infections by 83%, a modeling study suggested. If shared decision-making leads to fewer hepatitis B vaccinations, up to 1.8 million people could enter adulthood susceptible to infection, compared with 232,000 with a universal birth-dose policy. Shifting from a universal birth dose of the hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccine to recently proposed strategies of deferred vaccination or a shared decision-making approach could increase chronic HBV infections, according to projections from a modeling study. In a single-year U.S. birth cohort of 3.6 million infants, delaying the first vaccination dose until age 2 months would increase chronic HBV infections by 19% (255 to 303 cases), while the shared decision-making approach would increase chronic infections by 83% (467 cases), reported Amir Mohareb, MD, of Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, and colleagues in the Annals of Internal Medicineopens in a new tab or window. "These estimates suggest that the relative increase in HBV infections would be substantial, although the absolute increase would remain modest, at least in the early years after a policy change," they wrote. "If changes in CDC guidance result in an overall decrease in vaccine coverage, the effect on HBV infections will be even greater than what we report in the base-case scenario." If shared decision-making led to fewer HBV vaccinations, the result would be far more people entering adulthood susceptible to HBV infection -- up to 1,806,000, compared with 232,000 with a universal birth-dose scenario at year 20, Mohareb and team noted. "These results should motivate policymakers and clinicians to consider reimplementation of the prior recommendation for universal childhood HBV vaccination at birth." Ninety percent of perinatally exposed newborns will develop chronic HBV infection, and one in four people with untreated chronic HBV infection will develop complications such as cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma. Universal HBV vaccination at birth has been shown to be safe and effectiveopens in a new tab or window. Late last year, however, the CDC's revampedopens in a new tab or window Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices abandoned more than three decades of U.S. vaccine policy and voted to stop recommending a universal birth doseopens in a new tab or window. Instead, the panel recommended a shared clinical decision-making process for infants born to mothers who test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen. Under this guidance, parents and clinicians would decide "when or if" to administer the vaccine. For families opting not to give the birth dose, the panel suggested delaying the first dose until a child is 2 months old. The CDC's proposed childhood immunization scheduleopens in a new tab or window would subject HBV vaccination to shared clinical decision-making except in high-risk groups. Medical News from Around the Web 1 Live Science A fighter pilot had unexplained headaches for over a year, and the cause was hiding in plain sight — Diagnostic dilemma opens in a new tab or window 2 Harvard Health Radiofrequency ablation for back pain - Harvard Health opens in a new tab or window 3 Scientific American Can AI predict whether you’ll die from cancer from just an image of your face? opens in a new tab or window 4 Clinical Advisor Epilepsy Strongly Linked to Young-Onset Dementia opens in a new tab or window 5 NPR Expecting a baby? 5 tips to help you prepare for pregnancy costs opens in a new tab or window The current study's findings mirror the cautionary results of two similar modeling studies published earlier this year, which also warned of the potential dangers posedopens in a new tab or window by skipping the universal birth dose. In this study, Mohareb and colleagues also said that lower vaccination rates in delayed and shared decision-making scenarios could lead to even more chronic HBV infections by early adulthood. If vaccine uptake were 75% in a delayed-vaccination scenario, there would be 357 chronic infections, 40% more than the estimated 255 cases under a birth-dose scenario. A 26% vaccination rate with shared decision-making would mean 575 chronic HBV infections, 125% more than the birth-dose estimate. Delayed vaccinations would lead to an estimated 912,000 young adults susceptible to HBV infection, while shared decision-making would boost that number to 2,665,000. The authors also modeled a scenario that paired lower HBV birth-dose vaccination rates in infants of mothers who were HBV positive or had unknown HBV status with a greater population-wide HBV prevalence. In that scenario, deferred vaccination would result in 1,700 childhood chronic HBV infections, and shared decision-making would cause 2,192 such infections. Study limitations included no simulations of liver disease development or death, nor did the models predict immunity levels in children who received only one or two doses of the three-dose HBV vaccination series. The approval of GSK and Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ Hibsago for chronic hepatitis B virus infection has pushed open the flood gates for a handful of followers also hoping to offer a comparable or better options for patients with the intractable disease. Hibsago (bepirovirsen) is the first antisense oligonucleotide to receive an FDA nod for the indication. The therapy will offer a “functional cure,” meaning levels of the virus are pushed so low as to be undetectable. While partners GSK and Ionis may be the first, they won’t be the last, according to H.C. Wainwright analysts. “The first FDA approval of an antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B increases our confidence in the emerging functional cure market,” the firm wrote in a Thursday morning investor note. “We view approval as an important advance for the field: uncertainty over whether a finite regimen could generate sufficient sustained off-treatment responses to support FDA approval has now been resolved for bepi’s selected population.” Behind GSK and Ionis are about 16 companies, ranging from large caps like Gilead Sciences to smaller biotechs like Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals and Aligos Therapeutics. There are also a few privately held companies like Argo Biopharmaceuticals and Tune Therapeutics in the mix. Approvals GSK, Ionis win FDA nod for hepatitis B functional cure that controls virus after treatment Hibsago’s approval—a functional cure for certain patients with a hepatitis B infection—further validates Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ antisense platform, which has already generated two other new drug approvals this year. October 21, 2026 · 3 min read · Tristan Manalac Read more Many of these companies will present data at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) meeting in November. The approval of Hibsago “establishes a starting point for a multi-product market, in our view,” H.C. Wainwright wrote. The FDA granted Hibsago approval for a fairly complex indication. The drug can be used in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) therapy in adults with chronic hepatitis B infection who do not have liver damage. They must have been on the NRTI therapy for at least six months, have suppressed HBV DNA and have levels of hepatitis B virus (HBV) surface antigen below a certain threshold. The therapy was approved with a companion diagnostic from Roche to test for HBV surface antigen. With such a specific population, H.C. Wainwright points out that there are plenty of patients who do not fit the exact mold. “We believe higher-antigen patients and patients who do not achieve sustained responses remain substantial opportunities for subsequent regimens.” Aligos is one biotech that could offer such an option. The company is developing the oral capsid assembly modulator pevifoscorvir sodium (pevy) for patients with chronic infection who have a higher antigen burden. An abstract from AASLD shows a reduction in HBV surface antigen that H.C. Wainwright believes supports further exploration of whether the therapy could offer a functional cure for these patients. Investors will have to wait until the third quarter of 2027 for a more robust Phase 2 readout from the B-SUPREME trial, which H.C. Wainwright said is “the principal pevy efficacy checkpoint.” Precision Biosciences will also present at AASLD, showcasing Phase 1 results from the ELIMINATE-B program for the gene therapy PBGENE-HBV. While the data are early, H.C. Wainwright will be watching for details on the duration of pgRNA loss, which is the biomarker Precision is tracking to look for the elimination of the stable viral genomes that give rise to new HBV infections. GSK and Ionis will also have a showing at AASLD. H.C. Wainwright expects the presentation to help physicians understand how to select and manage patients. Arrowhead is another company that could benefit from the new market established by Ionis and GSK. The biotech’s siRNA daplusiran/tomligisiran is being tested by GSK in the Phase 2b B-UNITED trial along with Hibsago. Assembly Biosciences, which is developing the oral hepatitis D virus (HDV) entry inhibitor ABI-6250, is a “partnering opportunity,” according to H.C. Wainwright. Other names with early assets include Vir Biotechnology’s elebsiran and tobevibart combo and Mirum Pharmaceuticals’ monoclonal antibody brelovitug. “We would not transfer bepi’s HBV approval directly into higher efficacy assumptions for those programs,” H.C. Wainwright said. Leadership Vir Leans Into Immunology Roots After Flamed-Out COVID Fame Just a few months after Vir Biotechnology lost an emergency authorization for its COVID-19 antibody, Marianne de Backer stepped in as CEO to answer a critical question: What’s next? The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis. Image for illustration purposes Mega Doctor News - Advertisement - The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, in combination with existing antiviral therapy, to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in certain adults without cirrhosis. Hibsago is the first FDA-approved antisense oligonucleotide to treat chronic hepatitis B. Hibsago is approved for certain adults without cirrhosis who have been taking HBV antiviral therapy for at least six months, have suppressed levels of HBV in their blood and have hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) levels of 3,000 IU/mL or less, as determined by an FDA-authorized test. “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” said Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by HBV. Over time, the infection can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and increase the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago works by targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins, helping reduce the amount of virus and hepatitis B surface antigen in the body. - Advertisement - The FDA also authorized the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a companion diagnostic device to aid in the selection of patients with chronic HBV infection for treatment with antiviral therapy in accordance with the FDA approved drug labeling and to assist in monitoring patients throughout the course of treatment. Researchers studied Hibsago in two clinical trials that compared it with a placebo, an inactive treatment. Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. Patients take it alongside their existing hepatitis B medicine and continue that medicine for at least 24 weeks after their last Hibsago injection. Some patients may then be able to stop their existing medicine if they meet certain health and lab test requirements. Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood. Hibsago has a boxed warning for serious liver reactions as well as low platelet counts, which can increase the risk of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Hibsago also has warnings for worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, and serious risks if the injection is not administered properly. Patients need regular blood tests and follow up with their healthcare provider before and during treatment to monitor these risks. The most common side effects, excluding laboratory abnormalities, are injection site reactions, fever, fatigue and headache. - Advertisement - The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track and Breakthrough Therapy designations as well as Priority Review. The approval was granted to GSK plc. TRANSPORT SCIENCE & HEALTH SUBSCRIBE HOME Illnesses and conditions Breakthrough hepatitis B drug offers 'functional cure' for first time By Bronwyn Thompson October 21, 2026 Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Flipboard Email Breakthrough hepatitis B drug offers 'functional cure' for first time Life-changing hep b mediation approved by FDA Depositphotos View 1 Image 1/1 Life-changing hep b mediation approved by FDA Depositphotos For the first time, many people living with chronic hepatitis B may have a functional cure at hand. The US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved the Hibsago (bepirovirsen) injection, which studies show can keep the disease under control without the need for endless doses of antiviral drugs. Chronic hepatitis B (CHB) is a leading cause of cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), affecting more than 250 million people worldwide and causing upwards of a million deaths each year. Until recently, many of those with the condition have had no choice but to rely on long-term use of antiviral medication to keep CHB's viral load at bay. “For many people living with chronic hepatitis B, treatment can mean taking antiviral medication for years to keep the virus suppressed,” says Wendy Carter, DO, Acting Director of the Office of Infectious Diseases in the Center for Drug Evaluation and Research in the US. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended. This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” To qualify for this first-in-class treatment, individuals must meet a list of conditions, including being free of cirrhosis and on certain antiviral therapeutics for at least six months. According to the FDA, the approval of bepirovirsen was granted under the organization's Priority Review and Breakthrough Therapy Designation category, due to its significant improvement "over existing standard of care." “Despite current therapies, many people living with chronic hepatitis B remain on treatment indefinitely and continue to face the risk of serious liver complications," says Tony Wood, Chief Scientific Officer of the drug's production company, GSK. "For the first time, with Hibsago, US patients have the potential to achieve functional cure after a six-month treatment course, with the added convenience of the option of self-administration after the first dose.” "Functional cure" is key. It's not considered to be a complete cure, instead settling for HBV's DNA and viral protein – HBsAg – remaining undetected for 24 weeks once all other treatment has been stopped. This implies that the immune system has the disease under control without any ongoing intervention. Results from the B-Well phase III trials demonstrated "functional cure" rates of 19% in adults with ≤3000 IU/ml HBsAg, compared to current standard of care alone, which is less than 1% after 12 months. One in five might seem minimal, but it's a massive step forward in combating a deadly disease, and could potentially change – even save – the lives of millions. According to the FDA, "Across the two trials, 24% of patients who received Hibsago met the requirements to stop their existing medicine, compared with none who received placebo. Twenty-four weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients who received Hibsago still had the virus under control, and a protein that signals hepatitis B infection (HBsAg) could not be detected in their blood." CHB is reportedly the cause of an estimated 56% of liver cancers worldwide. While there is an effective vaccine against the disease, hesitancy towards it has grown, and other regions have inadequate access to such preventative medicines, resulting in the ongoing prevalence of hepatitis B. What's more, poor screening has hampered interventions to reduce liver damage over time, while efforts to block its major transmission route – perinatal transfer – have been complicated by myths and misinformation, particularly in the US. "This is the start of a new era in treating people living with CHB," says Dr. Norah Terrault, Chief of Gastroenterology & Hepatology, USC Keck Medical Center. “Bepirovirsen offers patients the potential to achieve functional cure after a short period of treatment, a long-standing goal for patients and physicians alike.” Source: GSK Tags Illnesses and conditionsFDALiver diseaseCancerhepatitis-bclinical trials Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Reddit Flipboard Email No comments Bronwyn Thompson Bronwyn has always loved words and animals, and she has the journalism and zoology degrees to prove it. Since 1992, we advocate for the rights and interests of people living with or affected by HIV/ AIDS and related co-infections within the WHO Europe region. EATG represents the diversity of more than 2,1 million people living with HIV in Europe and their communities. Learn more about us Our programmes Quality of Life Improving health-related quality of life and holistic well-being throughout the lives of people living with HIV Combination Prevention Increasing the usage of HIV, viral hepatitis, TB, and STI combination prevention and diagnostic strategies, especially in affected communities Partners in Science Ensuring that ongoing research continues to yield best quality new diagnostics, medicines, medical devices, care, as well as progress towards cure relative to HIV, viral hepatitis, TB, emerging infectious diseases, co-morbidities and STIs Latest activity News Blogs Resources Events Campaigns Calls & Vacancies Blogs October 22, 2026 Read more October 22, 2026 From standards to reality: EATG at the EACS Standard of Care Meeting in Budapest By Daniela Rojas Castro “Standards are written for people. They become reality when people help shape them, deliver them and check them!” Our Chair, Daniela Rojas Castro, represented EATG at the 7th EACS Standard of Care Meeting in Budapest on 8–9 October 2026. In her blog, she highlights the role of communities in advancing equitable, person-centred HIV care and calls for meaningful community engagement in developing, implementing and monitoring European standards. Read more Events Read more Stories That Built the HIV Movement: A Legacy Chest Screening Evening in Glasgow A community event organised by EATG to launch the Legacy Chest of Long-Term Survivors of HIV. Join us in Glasgow on 10 November 2026 for an evening of shared stories, food, drinks and conversation. EATG invites you to watch a selection of videos from the Legacy Chest, a growing archive of stories from long-term and lifetime survivors of HIV, created through our Long-Term Survivors of HIV project. Read more News October 1, 2026 Read more October 1, 2026 EATG’s strategic review 2026: Building the next chapter together EATG has published its Strategic Review Launch Report, documenting the discussions, findings, and initial priorities emerging from the Strategic and Governance Retreat held in Faro in June 2026. The report provides a detailed overview of the external and internal factors shaping EATG’s future, reflects on the organisation’s strengths and challenges, and sets out the key questions and next steps for the strategic review. It marks the beginning of a wider process that will involve EATG members, communities and stakeholders in shaping the organisation’s next strategic framework. Read more Publications October 1, 2026 Read more October 1, 2026 Strategic Review Launch Report (2026) The Strategic Review Launch Report, developed following EATG’s Strategic & Governance Retreat in Faro in June 2026, presents the findings and outputs of the first phase of the organisation’s strategic review. Read more Blogs September 30, 2026 Read more September 30, 2026 America First, One Year On: The IAS’s Responsibility “Civil society is losing the role it had in PEPFAR processes, community-based services are being scaled back and, in some countries, health agreements are becoming intertwined with strategic interests and negotiations over mineral resources. This is not country ownership. Suddenly transferring enormous costs to poor countries while simultaneously imposing conditions defined by the US government does not restore their sovereignty, just as replacing civil-society participation with negotiations between governments does not make the response more sustainable; it shifts power precisely when many HIV organisations are struggling to survive one of the most serious funding crises in decades.“ by Sandro Mattioli Read more News September 29, 2026 Read more September 29, 2026 EATG Launches the 2025 Annual Report Today, we are proud to publish the EATG Annual Report 2025, reflecting a year of significant achievements, important transitions and groundwork for the future. Read more Endorsements and Sign-ons September 17, 2026 Read more September 17, 2026 Formal Position of the NGO Delegation to the UNAIDS Programme Coordinating Board on the Future of UNAIDS EATG has endorsed the formal position of the NGO Delegation to the UNAIDS Programme Coordinating Board on the future of UNAIDS. The position remains open for endorsements. Read more Endorsements and Sign-ons September 9, 2026 Read more September 9, 2026 EU4Health Civil Society Alliance: Civil society stands together for sustainable funding for health civil society 187 civil society organisations (CSOs) from across Europe and sectors are standing together in support of EU health civil society and calling for the restoration of meaningful, adequate and predictable operating grants, under EU4Health and beyond. EATG endorses the statement. Read more Blogs September 8, 2026 Read more September 8, 2026 AIDS 2026 | A reflection on Rio: In search of a theme among promises for prevention “The big question is not whether researchers can get enough funding to do exploratory studies, but whether the world will be willing to provide the money for a cure for all, regardless of who they are and where they’re from. That question dominated the conference. My failure to find a theme was based on a feeling that all the busy research and science was pointless if the global will to apply it was missing.” by Gus Cairns Read more Blogs September 3, 2026 Read more September 3, 2026 AIDS 2026 | Let communities lead, for real: What presenting SCOPE at AIDS 2026 taught me “Evidence matters. Epidemiology matters. Biomedical innovation matters. But numbers cannot tell us everything about why a prevention technology that works perfectly in a clinical trial never reaches somebody who needs it. Communities often know why. We know which doors people are afraid to walk through. We know which language makes someone feel judged. We know why an intervention that looks excellent on paper might fail completely in a particular community. And when we do not know, we know that the first thing to do is ask. That knowledge is not supplementary to HIV expertise. It is HIV expertise.” by Amanita Calderón-Cifuentes Read more Blogs August 3, 2026 Read more August 3, 2026 United for Health at WorldPride in Amsterdam “I proudly represented EATG at the EMA (European Medicines Agency) Pride boat, carrying our main message loud and clear: United for Health. Because to fight injustice, we need to be healthy. To be healthy, we need love. And to stay strong, we need each other.” by Eliane Becks Nininahazwe Read more Events Read more The Silver Zone: A Networking Zone for Older People Living with HIV at AIDS 2026 EATG in partnership with Ribbon – A Center of Excellence, Realize, RNP+ Brasil, and Coletivo Loka de Efavirenz is co-organising “The Silver Zone: A Networking Zone for Older People Living with HIV” in the Global Village at the 26th International AIDS Conference (27 July – 31 July 2026) in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Read more News July 24, 2026 Read more July 24, 2026 EATG at AIDS 2026 EATG is happy to take part in the 26th International AIDS Conference (AIDS 2026) with four scientific posters and as a co-organiser of the Silver Zone in the Global Village. Read more News July 1, 2026 Read more July 1, 2026 SCOPE 2024-2026: Strengthening Community Voices in HIV Combination Prevention –Newsletter In its second funding cycle, EATG’s SCOPE project resumed activities from November 2024 to June 2026, partnering with community representatives to build capacity for delivering and advocating for community-led, integrated HIV prevention services. SCOPE strengthens community engagement at local and regional levels to reduce the gap in access and use of HIV combination prevention interventions by populations that are most affected by HIV, but which remain inadequately served by the health system and which are underrepresented in policy and public debate. This is a review of what we achieved together in this second cycle of SCOPE. Read more Blogs June 30, 2026 Read more June 30, 2026 SCOPE | Beyond Translation: Making Harm Reduction Information Accessible Across Europe (France, Poland and Portugal) With this project, EuroNPUD member organisations addressed a common issue: they wanted practical, trustworthy information in their own language. They wanted resources that reflected their own environments, their own services, and the challenges they face every day. This project therefore focused on more than translation. It focused on adaptation. by Leo Jefferys Read more Blogs June 26, 2026 Read more June 26, 2026 SCOPE | From Translation to Access: Why Language Matters in HIV Care (Turkey) Very quickly, it became clear that this wasn’t just about translating words. It was about translating meaning. Because in HIV, language carries a lot. It carries fear, stigma, medical complexity, and also reassurance, clarity, and empowerment. So, we didn’t just translate the text. We slowed things down, simplified where needed, added explanations, and included questions that people actually ask after diagnosis, the kind of questions that don’t always appear in clinical spaces, but come up in real life. While doing so, we ensured the knowledge was both culturally sensitive and thoughtfully localized, so it could genuinely reflect and respond to the needs of local communities. by Ozla Nuh Read more News June 22, 2026 Read more June 22, 2026 EATG to Join EMA’s “United for Health” Float at WorldPride 2026 EATG is proud to announce its participation in the European Medicines Agency’s (EMA) “United for Health” float during the WorldPride 2026 Canal Parade in Amsterdam on 1 August 2026. Read more News June 19, 2026 Read more June 19, 2026 EATG Endorses PICUM Statement and Calls for Health Safeguards in the EU Return Regulation The European AIDS Treatment Group (EATG) endorses the joint civil society statement led by PICUM, “No to EU law enabling home raids, policing of public services and racial profiling”, which, since earlier in 2026, has warned that the EU Return Regulation risks normalising surveillance, immigration raids, racial profiling, and the use of public services as instruments of migration enforcement. EATG shares its concerns regarding the impact of such measures on fundamental rights, public health, and access to treatment and care. Read more News June 18, 2026 Read more June 18, 2026 EATG General Assembly 2026: Building on Our Shared Commitment This year, EATG’s annual General Assembly (GA) took place virtually on May 29 and 30, bringing together members, staff, and leadership for two days of reflection, discussion, and decision-making focused on the organisation’s future. Read more Press releases and Statements June 5, 2026 Read more June 5, 2026 Press Release | HIV Long-Term Survivors Awareness Day: Survivors Gather in Sitges to Preserve Stories and Shape the Future As the world marks HIV Long-Term Survivors Awareness Day on June 5, a recent international gathering in Sitges, Spain, highlighted the power of storytelling, community, and lived experience in shaping the future of the HIV response. Read more News June 5, 2026 Read more June 5, 2026 Our Stories Built the Movement: Taking Stock of the HIV Long-Term Survivors Summit Outcomes on Survivors Awareness Day On the occasion of HIV Long-Term Survivors Awareness Day (5 June), we take stock of the outcomes and learnings from the recent HIV Long-Term Survivors Summit in Sitges, Barcelona. The Summit reflected that commitment in action, bringing together survivors and advocates to transform lived experience into collective learning, action and lasting impact. Read more Endorsements and Sign-ons June 3, 2026 Read more June 3, 2026 Joint Letter | Prioritising Better Health for All Europeans: A Call from the Health Community In the midst of negotiations on EU’s next long-term budget, more than 490 healthcare experts, scientists, academics, and patient advocates have sent a joint letter to EU leaders and national governments calling for health spending to be firmly protected and earmarked in the next MFF. EATG is proud to endorse this letter. Read more Publications May 27, 2026 Read more May 27, 2026 SCOPE: Multi Country Report | Monitoring the Implementation of HIV Combination Prevention at Country Level via the SCOPE Checklist EATG is publishing a community-led report on the implementation of HIV combination prevention in Italy, Armenia, Sweden, Slovenia, Ireland, Croatia, Turkey and Spain. Community-based organisations in these countries applied the SCOPE HIV Combination Prevention Checklist to assess both their own services and the broader national environment affecting key populations. Read more Events Read more SCOPE Closing Meeting: Take a Scoop! As the European AIDS Treatment Group’s SCOPE project comes to a close, we invite you to join us for an interactive online session to take stock of what we’ve achieved and collectively explore what comes next. Read more EATG Training Academy Capacity building is a key strategic approach for us. Our training projects and workshops aim to strengthen the knowledge and capacity of communities as well as to disseminate robust data and good practices. The EATG Training Academy website provides participants of trainings with all the information, support and resources they need. Since 1992, we advocate for the rights and interests of people living with or affected by HIV/ AIDS and related co-infections within the WHO Europe region. EATG represents the diversity of more than 2,1 million people living with HIV in Europe and their communities. Learn more about us Our programmes Quality of Life Improving health-related quality of life and holistic well-being throughout the lives of people living with HIV Combination Prevention Increasing the usage of HIV, viral hepatitis, TB, and STI combination prevention and diagnostic strategies, especially in affected communities Partners in Science Ensuring that ongoing research continues to yield best quality new diagnostics, medicines, medical devices, care, as well as progress towards cure relative to HIV, viral hepatitis, TB, emerging infectious diseases, co-morbidities and STIs Latest activity News Blogs Resources Events Campaigns Calls & Vacancies Blogs October 22, 2026 Read more October 22, 2026 From standards to reality: EATG at the EACS Standard of Care Meeting in Budapest By Daniela Rojas Castro “Standards are written for people. They become reality when people help shape them, deliver them and check them!” Our Chair, Daniela Rojas Castro, represented EATG at the 7th EACS Standard of Care Meeting in Budapest on 8–9 October 2026. In her blog, she highlights the role of communities in advancing equitable, person-centred HIV care and calls for meaningful community engagement in developing, implementing and monitoring European standards. Read more Events Read more Stories That Built the HIV Movement: A Legacy Chest Screening Evening in Glasgow A community event organised by EATG to launch the Legacy Chest of Long-Term Survivors of HIV. Join us in Glasgow on 10 November 2026 for an evening of shared stories, food, drinks and conversation. EATG invites you to watch a selection of videos from the Legacy Chest, a growing archive of stories from long-term and lifetime survivors of HIV, created through our Long-Term Survivors of HIV project. Read more News October 1, 2026 Read more October 1, 2026 EATG’s strategic review 2026: Building the next chapter together EATG has published its Strategic Review Launch Report, documenting the discussions, findings, and initial priorities emerging from the Strategic and Governance Retreat held in Faro in June 2026. The report provides a detailed overview of the external and internal factors shaping EATG’s future, reflects on the organisation’s strengths and challenges, and sets out the key questions and next steps for the strategic review. It marks the beginning of a wider process that will involve EATG members, communities and stakeholders in shaping the organisation’s next strategic framework. Read more Publications October 1, 2026 Read more October 1, 2026 Strategic Review Launch Report (2026) The Strategic Review Launch Report, developed following EATG’s Strategic & Governance Retreat in Faro in June 2026, presents the findings and outputs of the first phase of the organisation’s strategic review. Read more Blogs September 30, 2026 Read more September 30, 2026 America First, One Year On: The IAS’s Responsibility “Civil society is losing the role it had in PEPFAR processes, community-based services are being scaled back and, in some countries, health agreements are becoming intertwined with strategic interests and negotiations over mineral resources. The FDA has given the go-ahead to GSK and Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ antisense oligonucleotide bepirovirsen for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus infection, giving some patients the chance to potentially get off long-term medication. Bepiroversen, to be marketed under the brand name Hibsago, can help patients achieve undetectable levels of the virus in the blood after six months—serving as a functional cure, according to GSK’s announcement on Tuesday. GSK has forecasted peak worldwide sales of over £2 billion ($2.67 billion) for the drug, Reuters reported in May. BMO Capital Markets was more conservative in their estimate, projecting peak risk-unadjusted sales of $659 million in a Tuesday afternoon investor note. Ionis will receive 10–12% tiered royalties on GSK’s sales—about $163 million, by BMO’s estimate—a “relatively modest” contribution to the company’s commercial business, the analysts wrote. But the approval “adds meaningful validation” of Ionis’ antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) platform after recent setbacks to the overall class, BMO continued. The firm pointed to the Phase 3 failure of Ionis’ AstraZeneca-partnered ASO Wainua in transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) this summer and the September miss of Ultragenyx’s investigational ASO in Angelman syndrome. Rare diseases Ionis Paves Its Own Path as Initial Tryngolza Launch Defies Expectations Long an R&D company that partnered off assets, RNAi biotech Ionis Pharmaceuticals shifted in 2025 to bring two medicines to market alone. Analysts are already impressed—and there’s more to come in 2026. February 18, 2026 · 3 min read · Annalee Armstrong Read more Hibsago marks Ionis’ third ASO approval this year, following the September victory of Zanvastro for Alexander disease and the June clearance of Tryngolza to lower blood lipid levels and pancreatitis risk in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia. “While [Hibsago’s] approval was generally anticipated, we view this as another indication of the capabilities for the ASO platform Ionis has built,” BMO wrote. Hibsago is given via subcutaneous injection every six months, and patients have the option to self-administer the drug after the first dose. It is indicated for use in combination with nucleos(t)ide analog reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) and is approved for adult patients who have no liver scarring, according to GSK. Patients must have also been on NRTI treatment for at least six months and meet certain biomarker thresholds, as determined by an FDA-approved test. Alongside Hibsago’s approval, the agency cleared Roche’s Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a diagnostic device to identify patients with chronic hepatitis B who are eligible for treatment. The assay is also meant to help monitor patients while undergoing treatment. Originally developed by Ionis, Hibsago was licensed by GSK in August 2019 with $25 million upfront plus up to $262 million in milestones. The antisense therapy targets the genetic material of the hepatitis B virus and tags it for destruction. This mechanism prevents the virus’ replication, while also boosting the immune system’s capabilities to fight off the infection. The FDA previously granted Hibsago breakthrough and priority review designations. Hibsago’s approval was supported by data from the Phase 3 B-Well studies. The program consists of two late-stage studies, B-Well 1 and B-Well 2, which together enrolled more than 1,800 adults with chronic hepatitis B who had been exposed to NRTI treatment. Participants were given either Hibsago or placebo. Both trials primarily assessed for functional cure, defined as having no detectable levels of the virus for 24 weeks after ending all hepatitis B medication. Infectious disease GSK, Ionis’ hepatitis B functional cure effectively eliminates virus in nearly 20% of patients The antisense oligonucleotide was even more effective in patients with relatively low viral activity. More than one-quarter of these individuals had undetectable levels of the virus in the blood for at least six months after stopping treatment. May 28, 2026 · 2 min read · Tristan Manalac Read more Detailed findings from the B-Well studies presented in May showed that Hibsago resulted in a 19% functional cure response rate. None of the patients on placebo hit functional cure. In a key secondary analysis, GSK focused on patients with low baseline levels of the virus’ surface antigen. Hibsago treatment elicited a 26% functional cure rate in this subgroup, the pharma said on Tuesday. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended,” Wendy Carter, acting director of the FDA’s Office of Infectious Diseases under the Center for Drugs of Evaluation and Research, said in an agency release. “This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” As for safety, the FDA added a boxed warning on the Hibsago logo warning of serious liver reactions and low platelet counts, which the regulator said could aggravate the likelihood of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Other warnings for the drug include serious inflammatory side effects and declining kidney function. Based in Metro Manila, Tristan has more than eight years of experience writing about medicine, biotech and science. He can be reached at tristan.manalac@biospace.com, tristan@tristanmanalac.com or on LinkedIn. The approval of GSK and Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ Hibsago for chronic hepatitis B virus infection has pushed open the flood gates for a handful of followers also hoping to offer a comparable or better options for patients with the intractable disease. Hibsago (bepirovirsen) is the first antisense oligonucleotide to receive an FDA nod for the indication. The therapy will offer a “functional cure,” meaning levels of the virus are pushed so low as to be undetectable. While partners GSK and Ionis may be the first, they won’t be the last, according to H.C. Wainwright analysts. “The first FDA approval of an antisense oligonucleotide for chronic hepatitis B increases our confidence in the emerging functional cure market,” the firm wrote in a Thursday morning investor note. “We view approval as an important advance for the field: uncertainty over whether a finite regimen could generate sufficient sustained off-treatment responses to support FDA approval has now been resolved for bepi’s selected population.” Behind GSK and Ionis are about 16 companies, ranging from large caps like Gilead Sciences to smaller biotechs like Arrowhead Pharmaceuticals and Aligos Therapeutics. There are also a few privately held companies like Argo Biopharmaceuticals and Tune Therapeutics in the mix. Approvals GSK, Ionis win FDA nod for hepatitis B functional cure that controls virus after treatment Hibsago’s approval—a functional cure for certain patients with a hepatitis B infection—further validates Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ antisense platform, which has already generated two other new drug approvals this year. October 21, 2026 · 3 min read · Tristan Manalac Read more Many of these companies will present data at the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) meeting in November. The approval of Hibsago “establishes a starting point for a multi-product market, in our view,” H.C. Wainwright wrote. The FDA granted Hibsago approval for a fairly complex indication. The drug can be used in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NRTI) therapy in adults with chronic hepatitis B infection who do not have liver damage. They must have been on the NRTI therapy for at least six months, have suppressed HBV DNA and have levels of hepatitis B virus (HBV) surface antigen below a certain threshold. The therapy was approved with a companion diagnostic from Roche to test for HBV surface antigen. With such a specific population, H.C. Wainwright points out that there are plenty of patients who do not fit the exact mold. “We believe higher-antigen patients and patients who do not achieve sustained responses remain substantial opportunities for subsequent regimens.” Aligos is one biotech that could offer such an option. The company is developing the oral capsid assembly modulator pevifoscorvir sodium (pevy) for patients with chronic infection who have a higher antigen burden. An abstract from AASLD shows a reduction in HBV surface antigen that H.C. Wainwright believes supports further exploration of whether the therapy could offer a functional cure for these patients. Investors will have to wait until the third quarter of 2027 for a more robust Phase 2 readout from the B-SUPREME trial, which H.C. Wainwright said is “the principal pevy efficacy checkpoint.” Precision Biosciences will also present at AASLD, showcasing Phase 1 results from the ELIMINATE-B program for the gene therapy PBGENE-HBV. While the data are early, H.C. Wainwright will be watching for details on the duration of pgRNA loss, which is the biomarker Precision is tracking to look for the elimination of the stable viral genomes that give rise to new HBV infections. GSK and Ionis will also have a showing at AASLD. H.C. Wainwright expects the presentation to help physicians understand how to select and manage patients. Arrowhead is another company that could benefit from the new market established by Ionis and GSK. The biotech’s siRNA daplusiran/tomligisiran is being tested by GSK in the Phase 2b B-UNITED trial along with Hibsago. Assembly Biosciences, which is developing the oral hepatitis D virus (HDV) entry inhibitor ABI-6250, is a “partnering opportunity,” according to H.C. Wainwright. Other names with early assets include Vir Biotechnology’s elebsiran and tobevibart combo and Mirum Pharmaceuticals’ monoclonal antibody brelovitug. “We would not transfer bepi’s HBV approval directly into higher efficacy assumptions for those programs,” H.C. Wainwright said. Since 1992, we advocate for the rights and interests of people living with or affected by HIV/ AIDS and related co-infections within the WHO Europe region. EATG represents the diversity of more than 2,1 million people living with HIV in Europe and their communities. Learn more about us Our programmes Quality of Life Improving health-related quality of life and holistic well-being throughout the lives of people living with HIV Combination Prevention Increasing the usage of HIV, viral hepatitis, TB, and STI combination prevention and diagnostic strategies, especially in affected communities Partners in Science Ensuring that ongoing research continues to yield best quality new diagnostics, medicines, medical devices, care, as well as progress towards cure relative to HIV, viral hepatitis, TB, emerging infectious diseases, co-morbidities and STIs Latest activity News Blogs Resources Events Campaigns Calls & Vacancies Blogs October 22, 2026 Read more October 22, 2026 From standards to reality: EATG at the EACS Standard of Care Meeting in Budapest By Daniela Rojas Castro “Standards are written for people. They become reality when people help shape them, deliver them and check them!” Our Chair, Daniela Rojas Castro, represented EATG at the 7th EACS Standard of Care Meeting in Budapest on 8–9 October 2026. In her blog, she highlights the role of communities in advancing equitable, person-centred HIV care and calls for meaningful community engagement in developing, implementing and monitoring European standards. Read more Events Read more Stories That Built the HIV Movement: A Legacy Chest Screening Evening in Glasgow A community event organised by EATG to launch the Legacy Chest of Long-Term Survivors of HIV. Join us in Glasgow on 10 November 2026 for an evening of shared stories, food, drinks and conversation. EATG invites you to watch a selection of videos from the Legacy Chest, a growing archive of stories from long-term and lifetime survivors of HIV, created through our Long-Term Survivors of HIV project. Read more News October 1, 2026 Read more October 1, 2026 EATG’s strategic review 2026: Building the next chapter together EATG has published its Strategic Review Launch Report, documenting the discussions, findings, and initial priorities emerging from the Strategic and Governance Retreat held in Faro in June 2026. The report provides a detailed overview of the external and internal factors shaping EATG’s future, reflects on the organisation’s strengths and challenges, and sets out the key questions and next steps for the strategic review. It marks the beginning of a wider process that will involve EATG members, communities and stakeholders in shaping the organisation’s next strategic framework. Read more Blogs September 30, 2026 Read more September 30, 2026 America First, One Year On: The IAS’s Responsibility “Civil society is losing the role it had in PEPFAR processes, community-based services are being scaled back and, in some countries, health agreements are becoming intertwined with strategic interests and negotiations over mineral resources. Register here BioPharma, Pharma GSK Wins FDA Nod for Novel Hepatitis B Drug Offering a Potential Functional Cure GSK’s Hibsago brings a new mechanism of action to chronic hepatitis B, targeting the genetic instructions the virus uses to make copies of itself and viral proteins. This drug was licensed from antisense oligonucleotide specialist Ionis Pharmaceuticals. By Frank Vinluan on October 21, 2026 2:38 pm Share Share Options Share a link to this article Copy Link Copy Link Email Facebook LinkedIn X Chronic hepatitis B infection is currently managed with antiviral drugs that patients must take long-term, perhaps for life. The FDA has approved a new GSK drug that offers the potential for a six-month course of treatment and then nothing more. For these patients, the drug is able to knock the virus down to a level where the immune system regains control and keeps the infection in check — a functional cure. The FDA’s Tuesday regulatory decision brings a new product to GSK’s infectious disease portfolio, one offering a first-in-class approach expected to generate blockbuster sales. Known in development as bepirovirsen, GSK will market this drug under the brand name Hibsago. While hepatitis B virus can lead to an acute infection, it becomes chronic when the immune system is unable to clear the virus. An estimated 1.7 million people have chronic hepatitis B infection, which is associated with higher rates of liver cancer and death from all causes. Standard treatment is a chronic antiviral therapy that either inhibits viral DNA or stimulates an immune response against the virus. These drugs achieve low rates of functional cure, where signs of the virus can no longer be detected in the blood. presented by Sponsored Post Top 7 Modern AI-Powered EAP Providers for Global Workforces in 2026 Discover the top AI-powered EAP providers for 2026. Compare platforms like Kyan Health and Spring Health on triage speed, global reach, and clinical quality to transform workforce wellbeing. By Tiffany Cabasso, Operations Director, Kyan Health | Psychologist, FSP Hibsago works differently than the older antivirals. This new GSK drug is an antisense oligonucleotide designed to degrade the messenger RNA for hepatitis B virus, which in turn reduces levels of the virus’s DNA and viral proteins to a point where a patient’s immune system can regain control. Achieving a durable and sustained response could result in a functional cure. The regulatory submission for Hibsago was based on two placebo-controlled Phase 3 studies that evaluated the study drug, administered as a weekly injection, for up to 24 weeks. Participants in the trial were able to continue taking a standard of care hepatitis B antiviral medicine during the treatment period. During this period, patients who met certain lab and health test requirements were permitted to stop taking the existing antiviral. Across both studies, results showed 24% of patients who received Hibsago met requirements for stopping their existing medicine compared to none in the placebo arm. At 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B treatment, 19% of patients in the Hibsago arm had the virus under control. Also, a protein that signals hepatitis B infection could not be detected in their blood. Detailed results were presented in May during the European Association for the Study of the Liver (EASL) annual meeting and simultaneously published in the New England Journal of Medicine. The most common adverse reactions reported included injection site reactions, fever, and fatigue. Results also showed some patients had elevated levels of liver enzymes. A black box warning on Hibsago’s label instructs clinicians to conduct liver enzyme tests prior to starting treatment and periodically during the treatment period. The warning also flags a potential reduction in blood platelet levels that raises the risk of life-threatening bleeding. presented by Sponsored Post Closing the Quality-Affordability Gap in Workplace Mental Health In an interview, Kyan Health Co-Founder and Chief Commercial Officer Konstantin Struck discussed how Kyan gives mid-market and enterprise employers access to premium workforce mental healthcare, at a price point that is affordable. By Stephanie Baum The regulatory decision permits use of Hibsago in patients without liver cirrhosis. These patients must have been receiving antiviral therapy for at least six months to suppress levels of hepatitis B viral DNA. Eligible patients must also have hepatitis B surface antigen levels below a specified threshold, which is determined by a companion diagnostic. The FDA has authorized a Roche test to select patients for treatment with Hibsago. “Despite current therapies, many people living with chronic hepatitis B remain on treatment indefinitely and continue to face the risk of serious liver complications,” GSK Chief Scientific Officer Tony Wood said in a prepared statement. “For the first time, with Hibsago, U.S. patients have the potential to achieve functional cure after a six-month treatment course, with the added convenience of the option of self-administration after the first dose.” After the EASL presentation of Hibsago’s Phase 3 data in May, analysts at William Blair said they expected broad uptake of the drug. They noted that the current chronic hepatitis B market is worth $2.5 billion annually and the total addressable market is projected to grow to more than $7 billion by 2035. Leerink Partners said Hibsago offers blockbuster sales potential, but the bank cautioned that this drug’s uptake could be gradual given the testing and monitoring requirements for the therapy. Hibsago came from the labs of Ionis Pharmaceuticals, a specialist in antisense oligonucleotide drugs. Ionis and GSK began an infectious disease drug R&D alliance in 2010. GSK licensed the hepatitis B program from Ionis in 2019. Ionis is eligible receive milestone payments tied to the regulatory and commercial progress of the drug; the total payout could top $510 million, not including royalties from GSK’s sales of the new product. Hibsago was first approved in August in Japan. The drug is also currently under regulatory review in China. Illustration: libre de droit, via Getty Images

supplementary_news.content: Fierce Pharma Fierce Biotech Fierce Healthcare Fierce Life Sciences Events Advertise About Us Pharma Oncology Vaccines Asia Cell & Gene Therapy Drug Delivery Executives Manufacturing Facilities Recalls Warning Letters Marketing Special Reports Fierce 50 Special Report Awards Gala Trending Supply Chain AI and Machine Learning Awards Outsourcing Awards Innovation Awards AI Innovation Awards Pharma Marketing Awards Resources Podcasts Fierce Events Industry Events Webinars Whitepapers Survey Events Subscribe Subscribe Pharma Oncology Vaccines Asia Cell & Gene Therapy Drug Delivery Executives Manufacturing Facilities Recalls Warning Letters Marketing Special Reports Fierce 50 Special Report Awards Gala Trending Supply Chain AI and Machine Learning Awards Outsourcing Awards Innovation Awards AI Innovation Awards Pharma Marketing Awards Resources Podcasts Fierce Events Industry Events Webinars Whitepapers Survey Events Subscribe Fierce Pharma Fierce Biotech Fierce Healthcare Fierce Life Sciences Events Advertise About Us Pharma GSK brings promise of 'functional cure' to hepatitis B finish line with FDA nod for Hibsago By Fraiser Kansteiner Oct 21, 2026 6:39am GSK Ionis Pharmaceuticals chronic hepatitis B hepatitis B The FDA hailed Hibsago as a “first-of-its-kind” treatment in chronic hepatitis B, with the acting director of CDER’s Office of Infectious Diseases, Wendy Carter, adding that the approval “represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” (Eric Lalmand/Belga Mag/AFP/Getty Images) With the FDA’s green light in hepatitis B, GSK and its Ionis-licensed medicine bepirovirsen have racked up several notable distinctions, bringing the antisense oligonucleotide class to bear against the virus for the first time alongside the promise of functional cure-standard efficacy versus pre-existing treatments. Late Tuesday, the FDA gave the go-ahead to bepirovirsen to treat chronic hepatitis B (CHB) virus infection in tandem with nucleos(t)ide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (Nrtl) therapy in adults without cirrhosis. The drug will now carry the commercial moniker Hibsago and is specifically indicated in those who’ve already been taking Nrtl therapy for at least six months, and who have suppressed hepatitis B virus DNA and virus surface antigen levels no greater than 3000 IU/ml. GSK contends that the approval—delivered via FDA priority review and breakthrough therapy status—came in part through the recognition that its new hepatitis B treatment combo significantly ups the ante over standard-of-care nucleos(t)ide analogues, which include drugs like Bristol Myers Squibb’s Baraclude and Gilead Sciences’ Viread. That class of treatments can block the hepatitis B virus’ ability to replicate, cutting down viral numbers, but its potential to deliver a functional cure, which refers to the reduction of viral DNA and proteins to undetectable levels, is limited. “Despite current therapies, many people living with chronic hepatitis B remain on treatment indefinitely and continue to face the risk of serious liver complications,” Tony Wood, GSK’s chief scientific officer, said in a statement. “For the first time, with Hibsago, US patients have the potential to achieve functional cure after a six-month treatment course, with the added convenience of the option of self-administration after the first dose.” In its own approval announcement on Oct. 20, the FDA hailed Hibsago as a “first-of-its-kind” treatment in chronic hepatitis B, with the acting director of CDER’s Office of Infectious Diseases, Wendy Carter, adding that the approval “represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” The take was much the same among analysts at Jefferies, who wrote to clients Wednesday that the FDA check mark "validates the functional-cure opportunity," while caveating that safety and monitoring considerations may "cause debate" and make the drug's trajectory less certain in the real world. Related GSK’s Jemperli scores FDA approval in rectal cancer, backed by high complete response rate Chronic hepatitis B is a long-term liver infection caused by the hepatitis B virus (HBV) that, over time, can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis, and raise the risk of liver cancer. Hibsago, for its part, is designed to target the genetic instructions the hepatitis B virus uses to replicate and make viral proteins, ultimately curbing the overall amount of the virus and surface antigens in the body. GSK got its hands on the drug by way of a 2019 pact with Ionis Pharmaceuticals, with bepirovirsen becoming the recent centerpiece of a busy HBV pipeline after GSK last year shifted focus away from another functional cure candidate coded GSK3528869. Hibsago should be made available to U.S. patients before the end of the year, a GSK spokesperson told Fierce, adding that the drug’s list price will become public once pricing and reimbursement discussions have wrapped with payers. “We price our medicines according to the value and outcomes they bring to patients, providers and payers while being sensitive to current market and societal expectations,” the spokesperson said, flagging Hibsago’s functional cure-like efficacy and the fact that the price will reflect the medicine’s “significant clinical value.” The company will also be leveraging access and patient support programs to assist with Hibsago’s U.S. rollout. The FDA signed off on the drug after reviewing data from a pair of late-stage trials, B-Well 1 and B-Well 2, which each met their primary endpoint when Hibsago was tied to a statistically significant improvement in functional cure versus placebo in the overall study population. In detailed data from the program posted earlier this year, GSK said Hibsago allowed 19% of patients from that broad population to achieve its strictly defined functional cure criteria, which in the context of the studies was defined as hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) loss and undetectable HBV DNA for at least 24 weeks after the treatment. For the subgroup of patients with HBV surface antigen below the 1,000 international units per milliliter threshold at the trial’s start, the functional cure rate rose to 26%. With Hibsago's label confirmed to currently focus on patients already on therapy, as the Jefferies team predicted, the analysts said they continue to expect the drug to reach potential peak sales of 2.2 billion pounds sterling (around $2.95 billion). On safety and tolerability, meanwhile, GSK noted that Hibsago’s report card in its studies was “acceptable,” citing injection site redness, local pain and a “temporary rise in the blood level of a liver enzyme” as the most commonly recorded side effects. The drug will carry a boxed warning for serious liver reactions and low platelet counts, which can raise the risk of potentially fatal bleeding, the FDA noted in its approval announcement. Hibsago also carries warnings for worsening kidney function and serious inflammatory adverse reactions like vasculitis, plus the potential for other risks if the injection isn’t administered correctly. Patients will need regular blood tests and doctor follow-up before and during treatment to monitor for risks and side effects, the FDA added. That boxed warning, and monitoring requirements that the Jefferies team called "intensive" will likely prove the major test for Hibsago's launch, per the analysts' note Wednesday. The Jefferies team cautioned that the real-world treatment journey with GSK's new drug may be "less simple despite self admin." The analysts also spotlighted Hibsago's black box warning for both hepatic flares and thrombocytopenia, noting that the subsequent every-other-week or weekly monitoring burden patients will face could in turn "work against the commercial uptake and could slow adoption outside specialist hepatology centers." Nevertheless, the green light marks a major opportunity for GSK in the United States, where an estimated 1.7 million people are affected by chronic hepatitis B. However, the FDA nod is not Hibsago’s first. Initial global clearance for the medicine came by way of Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare in late August, with a similar functional cure label in adults with CHB already experienced with nucleos(t)ide analogues and who meet certain viral markers. Related GSK commits $800M to R&D, manufacturing hub, as Pennsylvania bonds deepen GSK is seeking approval of Hibsago in multiple territories, including Europe and China, and said Tuesday that it expects more regulatory decisions on the medicine to land “in the coming months.” “We are taking advantage of every regulatory pathway to accelerate the access of this medicine to patients,” Melanie Paff, Ph.D., GSK’s medical development leader for hep B, said on a media call about the bepirovirsen phase 3 data earlier this year.” Editor's note: This story has been updated with additional detail from an analyst note.
