supplementary_news.content_title: Ionis partner GSK announces Hibsago (bepirovirsen) approved in the U.S. for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B (CHB)
supplementary_news.content: Press Releases Ionis partner GSK announces Hibsago (bepirovirsen) approved in the U.S. for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) October 20, 2026 | 14 min read Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print – Approval based on Phase 3 data showing unprecedented functional cure rates compared to standard of care – – Six-month treatment with option of at-home administration after first dose – – CHB affects approximately 1.7 million people in the U.S. – CARLSBAD, Calif.--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Inc. (Nasdaq: IONS) partner GSK today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B (CHB) virus infection in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NrtI) therapy in adult patients without cirrhosis, receiving NrtI therapy for at least 6 months, who have suppressed HBV deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA), and with hepatitis B virus (HBV) surface antigen (HBsAg) levels ≤3000 IU/ml, as determined by an FDA-authorized test. GSK licensed bepirovirsen from Ionis and collaborated with them on its development. Bepirovirsen is a first in class RNA-targeted medicine that offers unprecedented functional cure rates compared to current standard of care. The approval was granted under FDA priority review and Breakthrough Therapy Designation, recognizing significant improvement of bepirovirsen and nucleos(t)ide analogue therapy over existing standard of care. “About 1.7 million people in the U.S are living with chronic hepatitis B, and yet treatment options have been historically limited and the vast majority of people living with the chronic infection require lifetime care without achieving meaningful functional cure,” said Brett P. Monia, Ph.D., chief executive officer, Ionis. “We are pleased to see the FDA approval of Hibsago, which adds to a growing portfolio of transformative medicines discovered and developed by Ionis that address serious diseases, including many that previously had limited or no available treatment options. We believe Hibsago will bring new hope to people living with chronic hepatitis B, offering the potential to achieve unprecedented functional cure rates after a six-month treatment course.” The approval was supported by results from the Phase 3 B-Well trials showing functional cure rates of 19% in adults with ≤3000 IU/ml HBsAg, compared to current standard of care alone, which typically achieves less than 1% functional cure rate after one year of treatment. Functional cure occurs when HBV DNA and HBsAg are undetectable for at least 24 weeks after stopping all treatment, indicating the disease is controlled by the immune system without medication. “This is the start of a new era in treating people living with CHB,” said Norah Terrault, MD, MPH, FAASLD, Chief of Gastroenterology & Hepatology, USC Keck Medical Centre. “Bepirovirsen offers patients the potential to achieve functional cure after a short period of treatment, a long-standing goal for patients and physicians alike." “CHB is a major public health challenge, affecting millions of people in the U.S. and accounting for approximately 56% of all global liver cancer cases,” said Chari Cohen, DrPH, MPH, president, Hepatitis B Foundation. “Today marks significant progress towards our aim of transforming the way CHB is managed with improvements in screening, diagnosis, and the availability of innovative treatment options for our community.” Quantitative surface antigen testing will support the diagnosis and identification of patients suitable for treatment with bepirovirsen who have baseline HBsAg levels ≤3000 IU/ml. Several tests are available, including a recently authorized FDA test. GSK continues to advance regulatory submissions for bepirovirsen across multiple geographies with key regulatory decisions anticipated in the coming months. GSK licensed bepirovirsen from Ionis in 2019 under a collaborative development and licensing agreement. Under the terms of the agreement, Ionis has received an upfront payment, license fee and development and regulatory milestone payments and is eligible to receive additional regulatory and sales milestone payments as well as tiered royalties of 10-12% on net sales of bepirovirsen. Results from the Phase 3 B-Well trials Pooled data from the Phase 3 B-Well trials showed that six-month treatment with bepirovirsen achieved a clinically meaningful 19% functional cure response rate (233 of 1,220 vs. 0 of 614 in the placebo group). B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 each met the primary endpoint, demonstrating a statistically significant improvement in functional cure versus placebo in the overall study population (adults with ≤3000 IU/ml HBsAg level). In a key secondary endpoint, a functional cure rate of 26% (200 of 768 vs. 0 of 393 in the placebo group) was achieved in participants with ≤1000 IU/ml HBsAg level, a group that represents approximately 45% of diagnosed CHB cases globally. Exploratory analyses also showed bepirovirsen reduced HBsAg to ≤100 IU/ml in 49% of participants (598 of 1220) in the overall study population, and in 62% of bepirovirsen recipients in the ≤1000 IU/ml (476 of 768) sub-group as of the week 72 visit. Medical literature has linked this low level of surface antigen with increased immune control and improved patient outcomes. The trials showed an acceptable safety and tolerability profile consistent with other studies of bepirovirsen. The three most frequently observed adverse events were injection site erythema, local pain and temporary rise in the blood level of a liver enzyme. About bepirovirsen Bepirovirsen is a non-GalNAc-conjugated antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) designed to recognize and inhibit the production of the genetic components (i.e., RNA) of the hepatitis B virus that can lead to chronic disease, potentially allowing a person’s immune system to regain control. Bepirovirsen reduces the production of RNA and viral proteins associated with HBV, suppresses the level of hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) in the blood, and may stimulate the immune system to increase the chances of a durable and sustained response. Bepirovirsen has been recognized by global regulatory authorities for its innovation and potential to address significant unmet need in hepatitis B, with Breakthrough Designation and priority review from the U.S. FDA, Breakthrough Therapy and Priority Review designation in China and SENKU designation in Japan. Bepirovirsen is approved in Japan and the U.S. INDICATION HIBSAGO is indicated in combination with nucleos(t)ide analogue reverse transcriptase inhibitor (NrtI) therapy to treat chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection in adults without cirrhosis who have been on NrtI therapy for ≥6 months with suppressed HBV DNA and who have HBV surface antigen (HBsAg) levels ≤3,000 IU/mL as determined by an FDA-authorized test. WARNING: ON-TREATMENT HEPATIC FLARES AND THROMBOCYTOPENIA On-Treatment Hepatic Flares HIBSAGO may cause on-treatment hepatic flares with increases in alanine aminotransferase (ALT) of >20-40x upper limit of normal (ULN) associated with decline in HBsAg. Some cases were associated with hyperbilirubinemia. Most occurred within the first 12 weeks and resolved when treatment was interrupted or discontinued. Do not initiate HIBSAGO in patients with evidence of acute hepatic impairment or cirrhosis. ALT and total bilirubin must be measured prior to treatment and frequently monitored during treatment. Treatment interruption, followed by dose reduction or discontinuation, may be necessary based on liver laboratory results. Thrombocytopenia HIBSAGO may cause reductions in platelet counts that may result in sudden and unpredictable thrombocytopenia, which can be life-threatening. Obtain platelet count prior to treatment; HIBSAGO is contraindicated in patients with platelet count <100 x 109/L. Monitor platelet counts at least weekly during treatment. Do not re-dose unless platelet count returns to ≥100 x 109/L. Permanently discontinue HIBSAGO if platelet count falls <50 x 109/L. CONTRAINDICATIONS HIBSAGO is contraindicated in patients: with acute hepatic impairment or cirrhosis who have mild, moderate, or severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh Class A, B, or C). with a platelet count <100 x 109/L prior to initiation of treatment. WARNINGS AND PRECAUTIONS On-Treatment Hepatic Flares Increases in ALT ≥3x ULN to 69x ULN were observed during treatment with HIBSAGO, most within the first 12 weeks. Isolated cases of ALT increases associated with an increase in total bilirubin resolved when treatment was permanently discontinued. Thrombocytopenia In addition to sudden and unpredictable thrombocytopenia, a gradual, dose-dependent decline in platelet count was observed in most patients that continued to worsen while on HIBSAGO. If a patient develops signs or symptoms of thrombocytopenia, pause HIBSAGO and obtain a platelet count as soon as possible. Instruct patients to report any symptoms of thrombocytopenia to their healthcare provider immediately. Consider the risks and benefits of treatment with HIBSAGO when treating patients who may be particularly susceptible to platelet count decreases. Worsening Renal Function Mean estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) declined within 4 weeks of initiation and continued to decline during treatment. These changes were generally reversible after treatment discontinuation. Obtain eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio (uACR) in all patients prior to initiation of treatment. Monitor eGFR frequently during and after treatment; treatment interruption or discontinuation may be necessary. Although no cases of glomerulonephritis were observed with HIBSAGO, glomerulonephritis has been observed with other antisense oligonucleotides; if suspected or confirmed, permanently discontinue HIBSAGO. Inflammatory and Immune Effects Influenza-like symptoms, laboratory test changes (e.g., decreases in complement factors C3 and C4), purpuric leg rashes, cutaneous leukocytoclastic vasculitis, dermatitis, pruritus/erythematous plaque, and polyarthralgia were observed. In addition, serious inflammatory and immune adverse reactions were reported, including immune thrombocytopenia, autoimmune hemolytic anemia, systemic inflammatory response syndrome, and a cryoglobulinemic flare. Consider the risks and benefits of HIBSAGO in patients who may be susceptible to inflammatory and immune effects, including solid organ transplant recipients, patients with autoimmune hepatitis, patients with a history of or conditions associated with vasculitis, or extrahepatic disorders related to HBV immune-mediated effects. If signs and symptoms suggestive of vasculitis/immune-associated events occur, and no alternative cause is identified, permanently discontinue treatment with HIBSAGO. Serious Adverse Reaction with Improper Administration Improper HIBSAGO administration, including not rotating injection sites, has been associated with the serious adverse reaction of omental infarction in one participant. Ensure injection sites are rotated from one week to the next and that the two injections making up each dose are separated by at least 2 inches (5 cm). Never inject into areas where the skin is tender, bruised, red, or hard. Post-Treatment Exacerbations of HBV Infection After NrtI Discontinuation Severe acute exacerbations of HBV infection may occur after discontinuation of anti-HBV therapy. If NrtI therapy is discontinued after completing HIBSAGO treatment, frequent monitoring is recommended for at least one year to detect acute exacerbations of HBV infection and the possible need for resumption of HBV treatment. Risk of human immunodeficiency virus-1 (HIV-1) Virologic Failure in Patients with HBV/HIV-1 Coinfection Who Discontinue NrtI Therapy Patients who are taking NrtI for HIV-1 and HBV coinfection must not stop taking their NrtI unless an HIV healthcare provider has directed them to do so. Risk of Hepatitis Flare in Patients with HBV/Hepatitis D Virus Coinfection HIBSAGO is not recommended in patients with HDV coinfection due to the potential for an exacerbated risk of clinically significant ALT increases. Unknown Effect on Preventing Transmission of HBV There are no data on the effect of HIBSAGO in preventing transmission of HBV. Patients must be advised to use appropriate precautions to prevent transmission of HBV. ADVERSE REACTIONS The most common adverse reactions (≥10%), excluding laboratory abnormalities, reported with HIBSAGO included injection site reactions, pyrexia, fatigue, and headache. Selected laboratory abnormalities worsened from baseline, including but not limited to, increases in ALT and total bilirubin, decreases in platelets and eGFR. DRUG INTERACTIONS Monitor patients for signs of bleeding and thrombocytopenia if HIBSAGO is taken concomitantly with anticoagulants, antiplatelets, or drugs that decrease platelet count. Monitor patients for signs of worsening renal function during concomitant administration of HIBSAGO with drugs that may impair renal function. Concomitant administration of HIBSAGO and peginterferon alfa-2a is not recommended due to the potential for an exacerbated risk of increased ALT, decreased platelet count, and immune-mediated effects. USE IN SPECIFIC POPULATIONS Pregnancy and Lactation There are insufficient data on HIBSAGO use in pregnancy or during breastfeeding. Consider the benefits of breastfeeding together with the mother’s clinical need for HIBSAGO. Pediatric Use HIBSAGO’s safety and effectiveness have not been established in patients under 18 years of age. Renal Impairment HIBSAGO can cause worsening renal function. No dosage adjustment is needed for mild renal impairment. Data are insufficient for moderate or severe renal impairment or end-stage renal disease (ESRD). Please see full Prescribing Information, including Boxed Warning, for HIBSAGO. Please see accompanying U.S. Prescribing Information here . About B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 B-Well 1 (NCT05630807) and B-Well 2 (NCT05630820) trials are global multi-center, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials conducted in 29 countries. They assessed the efficacy, safety, pharmacokinetic profile, and durability of functional cure in nucleos(t)ide analogue-treated adult participants with chronic hepatitis B and baseline surface antigen (HBsAg) ≤3000 IU/ml. The primary endpoint assessed the proportion of participants achieving functional cure in patients with baseline HBsAg ≤3000 IU/ml (assessed six months after all therapies were discontinued). A key ranked secondary endpoint evaluated functional cure in participants with baseline HBsAg ≤1000 IU/ml. About Chronic Hepatitis B (CHB) Hepatitis B is a viral infection that can cause both acute and chronic liver disease. Chronic hepatitis B occurs when the immune system is unable to clear the virus, resulting in long-lasting infection that affects more than 240 million people worldwide. The disease causes approximately 1.1 million deaths each year, and accounts for approximately 56% of liver cancer cases globally. Currently, many patients often require lifelong antiviral therapy for viral suppression, making functional cure a critical goal in disease management. About Ionis Pharmaceuticals, Inc. For more than three decades, Ionis has invented medicines that bring better futures to people with serious diseases. Ionis currently has marketed medicines and a leading pipeline in neurology, cardiometabolic disease and select areas of high patient need. As the pioneer in RNA-targeted medicines, Ionis continues to drive innovation in RNA therapies in addition to advancing new approaches in gene editing. A deep understanding of disease biology and industry-leading technology propels our work, coupled with a passion and urgency to deliver life-changing advances for patients. To learn more about Ionis, visit Ionis.com and follow us on X (Twitter) , LinkedIn and Instagram . supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Home Conditions Back Conditions View All ADD/ADHD Allergies Arthritis Atrial fibrillation Breast Cancer Cancer Crohn's Disease Depression Diabetes DVT Eczema Eye Health Heart Disease HIV & AIDS Hypertension Lung Disease Lupus Mental Health Multiple Sclerosis Migraine Pain Management Psoriasis Psoriatic Arthritis Rheumatoid Arthritis Sexual Conditions Skin Problems Sleep Disorders Ulcerative Colitis View All Drugs & Supplements Back Drugs & Supplements Drugs & Supplements Pill Identifier Interaction Checker Pet Medications Well-Being Back Well-Being Aging Well Baby Birth Control Children's Health Diet & Weight Management Fitness & Exercise Food & Recipes Health & Balance Healthy Beauty Men's Health Parenting Pet Health Pregnancy Sex & Relationships Teen Health Women's Health Symptom Checker Find a Doctor More Back More News Health Tools Blogs Podcasts Webinars Newsletters Videos WebMD Surveys WebMD Magazine Best Hospitals Support Groups Privacy & More Subscribe Log In Subscribe Drugs & Supplements/ Drug Updates/ FDA Approves Hibsago: A New Treatment for Chronic Hepatitis B Written by Mary Windle, PharmD Published on October 22, 2026 3 min read What Is Hibsago and How Does It Work? The FDA has approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen) for adults with long-term hepatitis B virus infection who do not have liver scarring, also called cirrhosis. It is meant for patients who have already been taking daily antiviral pills for at least six months, have low levels of virus in their blood, and have low amounts of a viral protein called surface antigen. Hibsago must be used alongside a patient's existing antiviral pills. Hepatitis B is a virus that causes a lasting infection in the liver. Over time, it can harm the liver and lead to liver cancer or severe liver damage. Current treatments usually involve taking antiviral medicine daily for many years or even for life to keep the virus quiet. Hibsago works in a new way compared to older drugs. It targets the genetic signals that the hepatitis B virus uses to copy itself and build viral proteins. By blocking these signals, Hibsago lowers the amount of virus and viral proteins in the body. This may help the patient's immune system control the infection on its own, allowing some patients to safely stop all hepatitis B medicines. Why Was Hibsago Approved? The FDA approved Hibsago based on results from two large clinical trials called B-Well 1 and B-Well 2. The studies looked at more than 1,800 adults with chronic hepatitis B who were taking daily antiviral pills. Patients received either Hibsago injections or a placebo (an inactive treatment with no medicine) for 24 weeks while continuing daily treatment with their hepatitis B pills. In these studies, Hibsago significantly helped more patients achieve viral control than placebo. Overall, 19% of patients who took Hibsago were able to stop all hepatitis B treatments and keep the virus at undetectable levels 24 weeks after stopping treatment. In comparison, none of the patients who took the placebo reached this goal. Among patients who started with lower levels of the hepatitis B surface antigen protein, 26% achieved this viral response. While Hibsago helped control the virus, it also showed important safety risks during the trials. Some patients had sudden drops in blood platelets, which are cells that help stop bleeding. Others had temporary spikes in liver enzymes, which can happen as the immune system fights the virus. Healthcare providers closely track these safety signs through blood tests during treatment. What Do I Need to Know About Hibsago? Hibsago is given as an injection under the skin of the thigh, stomach, or upper arm. Patients receive doses twice a week for the first two weeks, and then once a week through week 24. A healthcare provider gives the first injection and teaches the patient or caregiver how to give doses at home. Each weekly dose usually requires two separate injections given at least 2 inches apart. Patients must continue taking their daily antiviral pills during Hibsago treatment and for at least 24 weeks after completing treatment before a healthcare provider decides if it is safe to stop pills. Before starting Hibsago and while taking it, patients need regular blood tests to monitor their liver enzymes, platelet counts, and kidney function. You should not take Hibsago if you have cirrhosis, active liver failure, or very low blood platelet counts. Tell your healthcare provider if you have kidney problems, a history of autoimmune disease, or if you also have HIV, hepatitis C, or hepatitis D. The most common side effects of Hibsago are mild to moderate injection site reactions, such as redness, pain, bruising, or swelling where the shot was given. Other common side effects include fever, fatigue, headache, and muscle aches. Contact your healthcare provider immediately if you develop signs of liver problems (such as yellowing skin or eyes, dark urine, or stomach pain) or signs of low platelets (such as unusual bruising, bleeding gums, nosebleeds, or blood in your urine or stool). It is not known if Hibsago is safe for a fetus or if it passes into breast milk. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, talk to your healthcare provider to discuss the risks and benefits. Taking Hibsago also does not prevent you from spreading the hepatitis B virus to others, so you should continue taking precautions to protect sexual partners and family members. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Thursday, October 22, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Cancer ANKRD11 restrains CD8+ T cells in hepatitis B and cancer models by October 22, 2026 in Cancer Reading Time: 2 mins read 0 ANKRD11 restrains CD8+ T cells in hepatitis B and cancer models Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Researchers have identified ANKRD11 as a regulator that restrains CD8+ T-cell responses in experimental models of chronic hepatitis B virus infection and cancer. A team led by Zhou Xuyu of the Institute of Microbiology at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, with collaborators from Beijing Ditan Hospital and Capital Medical University, reported that the protein limits the activity of these infection-fighting immune cells by suppressing the AP-1 signaling pathway. The peer-reviewed study, published in Nature Immunology on September 11, found that removing ANKRD11 from T cells enhanced their capacity to respond to infected and cancerous cells in mice. The work used a mouse model designed to reproduce key features of human immune responses to HBV. Chronic HBV infection affects an estimated 296 million people worldwide and can lead to serious liver disease, including cirrhosis and liver cancer. In the study’s model, CD8+ T cells normally weaken during persistent infection, multiply less effectively and become less able to attack virus-infected cells. The researchers combined whole-genome genetic screening with functional experiments to identify genes that could influence T-cell responses during chronic infection. Ankrd11 was selected for further study because it emerged as a strong candidate and had not previously been characterized as a regulator of this response. Deleting Ankrd11 specifically in T cells did not measurably impair their development, but it substantially increased their antiviral and antitumor activity. The altered cells produced higher levels of key immune molecules and attacked infected and cancerous cells more effectively. Gene-expression analysis indicated that pathways associated with T-cell function were more readily activated when ANKRD11 was absent. The researchers also found that ANKRD11-deficient T cells were more resistant to signals that normally dampen immune responses. Together, these observations support the conclusion that ANKRD11 acts as a molecular brake on CD8+ T-cell activity, with AP-1 signaling among the pathways restrained by the protein. In HBV-infected mice, selective removal of Ankrd11 from T cells resulted in more active immune cells within the liver, improved viral clearance and better disease outcomes. Separate experiments in another viral infection model and a cancer model showed that T cells lacking Ankrd11 could better control infection and shrink tumors, including in settings where other treatments had failed. Combining the approach with existing therapies produced a stronger effect in the researchers’ experiments. These findings provide preclinical evidence that targeting ANKRD11 may help restore immune activity in chronic infection and cancer, but the work was conducted in mouse models and does not establish safety or effectiveness in people. Any therapeutic use would require additional studies and clinical evaluation. supplementary_news.excerpt: The US FDA has approved GSK’s Hibsago for chronic hepatitis B, with 19% of trial participants achieving a functional cure.

supplementary_news.content_title: Hepatitis B Breakthrough: GSK's New Drug Hibsago Helped 19% Stay Off Treatment
supplementary_news.content: Highlights: - The US FDA approved GSK's Hibsago (bepirovirsen) on October 20, 2026, for certain adults with chronic hepatitis B - About 19% to 20% of patients achieved a functional cure 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B medicines in Phase 3 trials - The drug carries serious warnings for liver reactions and low platelet counts, so patients need regular blood tests and medical supervision People with chronic hepatitis B may need to take antiviral tablets every day for many years, sometimes for life. These medicines control the virus, but they rarely clear it completely. If treatment is stopped, the virus can return. A new drug may give some patients a chance to remain off treatment. On October 20, 2026, the US FDA approved Hibsago (bepirovirsen), developed by GSK. It is an injection given under the skin alongside existing hepatitis B tablets. It is the first approved drug of its kind, known as an antisense oligonucleotide, for chronic hepatitis B(). The approval was based mainly on two large clinical trials, B-Well 1 and B-Well 2, published in the New England Journal of Medicine in 2026. The results showed that 19% to 20% of patients who received bepirovirsen achieved a functional cure by week 72, compared with none who received a placebo(). A placebo is a treatment that does not contain the active drug. However, around 4 in 5 patients did not achieve a functional cure. The drug also carries serious risks and requires close monitoring. Understanding who may benefit, how the treatment works and what the risks are is important before considering it. What Did the B-Well Studies Find? The B-Well 1 and B-Well 2 trials tested whether bepirovirsen could help people with chronic hepatitis B remain off their usual medicines. The studies were funded by GSK and reported by Hou and colleagues in the New England Journal of Medicine. Researchers conducted two similar trials to check whether the results were consistent. Together, the studies included about 1,838 adults, although the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) reported 1,834 participants in its main analysis(). How the B-Well Trials Were Designed Study detail What it means Participants Adults with chronic hepatitis B who did not have cirrhosis, or advanced scarring of the liver. Number of participants About 1,838 across both trials. Study locations 29 countries across Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Americas. Existing treatment Participants were already taking stable antiviral tablets, known as nucleos(t)ide analogue (NA) therapy. Starting HBsAg level More than 100 and up to 3,000 IU/mL. HBsAg is a protein found in the blood that signals hepatitis B infection. Study treatment Bepirovirsen 300 mg injected under the skin every week for 24 weeks, or a placebo. Treatment allocation For every two patients receiving bepirovirsen, one received a placebo. Stopping existing tablets Eligible patients stopped their usual hepatitis B tablets at week 48. Main outcome Whether patients achieved a functional cure by week 72, which was 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B medicines. What Does a Functional Cure Mean? A functional cure does not mean that every trace of the virus has been removed from the body. It means that the infection remains under control even after treatment ends. For the B-Well trials, patients had to meet three conditions at week 72: - Very low virus levels: Hepatitis B virus DNA (HBV DNA) had to remain below the test's detection limit. - No detectable HBsAg: The hepatitis B surface antigen, a protein linked to the infection, had to be absent from the blood test. - No additional treatment: Patients could not need rescue treatment to achieve these results. In simple terms, patients had to remain in control of the infection for 24 weeks after stopping all hepatitis B medicines. Functional Cure Rates in the B-Well Trials Trial Bepirovirsen group Placebo group B-Well 1 20% (127 of 650 patients) 0 of 328 patients (0%) B-Well 2 19% (106 of 570 patients) 0 of 286 patients (0%) Across both trials, 233 of 1,220 patients who received bepirovirsen achieved a functional cure. That is about 19 out of every 100 patients. No patient in either placebo group achieved this outcome. The results are encouraging, but most patients did not achieve a functional cure. This is an important point for anyone considering the treatment. What Side Effects Did the Trials Report? Safety measure Bepirovirsen Placebo Any side effect 91% 73% Serious side effects 7% 4% Severe side effects during treatment (Grade 3 or higher) 16% 3% Severe rise in ALT, a liver enzyme 6% Not specified These figures show that side effects were more common among patients who received bepirovirsen. Grade 3 or higher side effects are events classified as severe or worse. The researchers concluded that bepirovirsen helped more patients achieve a functional cure than the placebo, allowing some to remain off their usual hepatitis B medicines. Who Can Receive Hibsago Under the FDA Approval? Patients must meet the following conditions: - No cirrhosis: They must not have cirrhosis, which is severe scarring of the liver. - Existing treatment: They must have taken hepatitis B antiviral medicines for at least six months. - Virus under control: Their hepatitis B virus levels must already be suppressed in the blood. - Suitable HBsAg level: Their HBsAg level must be 3,000 IU/mL or lower, measured using an FDA-authorised test. The FDA also approved a blood test called the Roche Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay. It measures the amount of HBsAg in the blood and helps doctors select suitable patients and monitor treatment. Hibsago Treatment and Follow-Up Steps Step What happens 1. Injections Hibsago is injected under the skin for up to 24 weeks. 2. Continue tablets Patients continue their usual hepatitis B antiviral tablets during the injection course. 3. Continue treatment after injections Patients keep taking their tablets for at least another 24 weeks after the last injection. 4. Assess whether tablets can stop Eligible patients may stop their tablets only after meeting the required health and blood test criteria. 5. Check the outcome Doctors monitor patients to see whether the virus remains under control after all treatment has stopped. Patients must not stop their existing hepatitis B medicines on their own. Any decision to stop treatment must follow the approved criteria and a doctor's assessment. What Warnings Did the FDA Issue? Hibsago carries a boxed warning, the FDA's strongest type of safety warning, for two serious risks: - Serious liver reactions: Changes in liver enzymes may require urgent assessment and treatment. - Low platelet counts: Platelets help blood clot. Very low levels can increase the risk of serious bleeding. The drug also carries warnings about worsening kidney function, serious inflammatory reactions such as vasculitis, and serious risks associated with incorrect administration. Common side effects include injection-site reactions, fever, tiredness and headache. Patients need regular blood tests and medical follow-up before and during treatment. The FDA granted Hibsago Fast Track, Breakthrough Therapy and Priority Review status. These programmes help speed the review of certain medicines. An FDA official said the treatment offers some patients the possibility of controlling the virus after all treatment has ended. What Does the Hepatitis B Foundation Say About the Approval? The Hepatitis B Foundation, a US nonprofit organisation that supports hepatitis B research and patient advocacy, welcomed the approval on October 20, 2026. The Foundation highlighted three important points(): - A new treatment option: Hibsago is the first approved drug reported to offer some people with chronic hepatitis B a chance of a functional cure. - A major development: It is the first new hepatitis B therapy approved in the US in 10 years. - A chance, not a guarantee: The trials found a potential functional cure in about 20% of patients. The Foundation estimates that about 2.4 million people in the US live with chronic hepatitis B. It also says hepatitis B accounts for about 56% of liver cancer cases worldwide. Hepatitis B is one of the world's most common serious liver infections. More than one million people die from it each year, although the infection can be prevented through vaccination and treated with medicines. It is often called a silent epidemic because many people have no symptoms. They may not know they are infected, even as the virus damages their liver, and may unknowingly pass the infection to others. What Advice Does the Foundation Give? - People living with chronic hepatitis B should discuss their treatment options with their doctor and ask whether bepirovirsen may be suitable for them. - People who have never been tested should ask about hepatitis B screening. - Health systems should strengthen screening, vaccination and access to care for people who test positive. A new treatment can help only if people know they have the infection and can access medical care. What Do Liver Specialists Say About Hibsago? The physicians described the trial results as an important step because current hepatitis B tablets control the virus but rarely clear HBsAg. As a result, many patients need long-term treatment. A functional cure may reduce the risk of liver disease progressing and could lower the risk of liver cancer. It may also reduce the cost, daily burden and risk of missed doses associated with lifelong treatment. What Doctors May Need to Do When Using Bepirovirsen Area What it means for patients Measure HBsAg Doctors need a quantitative HBsAg test, which measures the exact amount of the surface antigen in the blood. Patients with levels at or below 1,000 IU/mL responded better in the trials. Frequent blood tests Patients in the trials were checked every one to two weeks. Doctors will need to monitor platelet counts and kidney function, including eGFR, a measure of how well the kidneys filter blood. Check treatment milestones Eligible patients who meet the trial's criteria can stop their tablets at week 48. Their response is then assessed at week 72. Watch liver enzymes Doctors need to assess increases in ALT, a liver enzyme that can rise when liver cells are damaged or inflamed. Are Liver Enzyme Rises Always a Sign of Damage? About 24% of patients had ALT levels at least three times the upper limit of normal during treatment. Dr Kwo explained that these rises may be linked to the immune system attacking infected cells and clearing the infection, rather than direct drug damage in every case. However, an ALT rise must never be assumed to be harmless. Doctors need to assess each patient carefully to decide whether the change is an expected immune response or a sign of a serious liver problem. Which Patients Need Extra Caution? The findings should not automatically be applied to people who were not covered by the trials, including: - People with advanced cirrhosis. - People also infected with HIV, hepatitis C or hepatitis D. - People with HBsAg levels above 3,000 IU/mL. The expert summary also notes that severe side effects occurred in 16% of patients receiving bepirovirsen. Drops in platelet counts and kidney function were reported to move back towards normal after the drug was stopped. Doctors still need more information about how long a functional cure lasts over many years. Researchers are also exploring whether combining bepirovirsen with other treatments could improve cure rates beyond 20%. How Does Bepirovirsen Work? A review by Woo and Heo in Future Virology explains how bepirovirsen works and summarises findings from earlier studies(). Bepirovirsen is an antisense oligonucleotide, a short piece of genetic material designed to attach to specific genetic messages. In simple terms, it targets the instructions the hepatitis B virus uses to make its proteins and reproduce. By interfering with these instructions, the drug can reduce HBV DNA and HBsAg. The review also describes its potential to help the immune system clear infected liver cells. What Did Earlier Studies Find? Study stage or area Main finding Phase 1 The drug was absorbed quickly and spread through the body. It did not build up in the blood, and little was removed through the kidneys. The review reported that its behaviour was not affected by hepatitis B tablets or liver function. Phase 2 HBsAg and HBV DNA levels fell. About 6% of patients overall maintained undetectable levels after treatment ended. Dose selected for Phase 3 300 mg injected weekly for 24 weeks. Best predictor of response The starting HBsAg level. Lower levels were linked to better outcomes. Safety The most common side effect was a reaction at the injection site. Combination treatment Combining bepirovirsen with existing tablets or peginterferon did not produce high cure rates in the earlier studies. The review noted that further research may still expand treatment options. The phase 2 studies found a functional cure in about 6% of patients overall, while the phase 3 trials reported around 19% to 20%. However, the studies were not identical. The later trials selected patients within a specific starting HBsAg range of more than 100 and up to 3,000 IU/mL. This suggests that choosing the right patients is important when using bepirovirsen. The review also noted that the drug was the first of its kind to reach phase 3 clinical trials. What Happens When Patients Stop Hepatitis B Tablets Without a New Drug? Some people with chronic hepatitis B stop their antiviral tablets under medical supervision, even without bepirovirsen. A review by Medas and colleagues in the World Journal of Clinical Cases explains the possible benefits and risks of this approach(). The usual tablets are called nucleos(t)ide analogues, or NUCs. They are widely used to control hepatitis B and help patients live longer. However, they often do not remove cccDNA, a form of viral genetic material that can remain inside liver cells. This is one reason why many patients need long-term treatment. Patients may want to stop because of the cost, possible side effects and the daily burden of taking medicines. But stopping can allow the virus to return. How Often Does HBsAg Disappear With Tablets Alone? The review found that HBsAg loss during tablet treatment was uncommon, at about 1.02% per year. HBsAg loss can also occur without treatment, but estimates vary from 0.12% to 2.38%. What Have Studies Found After Patients Stop Tablets? Study group Reported HBsAg loss How to understand the result European study About 25% at 18 months About 25 out of every 100 patients lost HBsAg by 18 months. Other studies 19% at 3 years; 20% at 4 years; 39% at 5 years Results varied considerably between studies and follow-up periods. Asian studies 13% at 5 years; 16% at 6 years HBsAg loss was reported in a smaller proportion of patients in these studies. Multicentre study 14.8% in non-Asian patients and 1.5% in Asian patients The reported rates differed between the two groups. These figures come from different studies, so they should not be treated as directly comparable. They show that HBsAg loss after stopping tablets can happen, but the likelihood varies between patient groups and studies. What Does the New Drug Hibsago Mean for India? An editorial by Swaroop, Shalimar and Acharya in the Indian Journal of Gastroenterology describes the global and Indian hepatitis B burden.() How Big Is the Hepatitis B Problem Worldwide? Measure Reported figure What it means People living with hepatitis B in 2022 254 million About 254 million people worldwide were living with chronic hepatitis B. Share of viral hepatitis deaths linked to hepatitis B 83% Hepatitis B caused most of the reported deaths from viral hepatitis. People diagnosed 13% Only about 13 out of every 100 people living with chronic hepatitis B had been diagnosed. People receiving treatment 3% Only about 3 out of every 100 people living with chronic hepatitis B were receiving treatment. Hepatititis Vaccination: What Progress Has India Made? India launched the National Viral Hepatitis Control Program in 2018. Hepatitis B vaccination has improved, with coverage of the third vaccine dose reaching about 93% in 2023. However, birth-dose coverage was about 63%, leaving room for improvement. The editorial calls for better data collection, stronger tracking of patients, wider access to testing and antiviral medicines, and greater involvement of private healthcare providers. For India, the first challenge is finding people who have hepatitis B and connecting them to care. A new drug can help only those who are diagnosed and meet its treatment requirements. The sources reviewed here do not confirm whether Hibsago will be available in India or how much it may cost. Who May Benefit, and What Should Patients Ask Their Doctor? The study results are most relevant to adults with chronic hepatitis B who do not have cirrhosis, have already been taking antiviral tablets and meet the required blood test criteria. Who May Be Suitable? - Adults with chronic hepatitis B who do not have cirrhosis. - People who have taken antiviral tablets for at least six months and whose virus levels are suppressed. - People whose HBsAg level is 3,000 IU/mL or lower. The B-Well trials included patients with starting levels above 100 and up to 3,000 IU/mL. - People who can attend regular appointments and complete the required blood tests. Patients with HBsAg levels below 1,000 IU/mL had better results in the trials. However, this does not guarantee that an individual patient will achieve a functional cure. Who Was Not Covered by the Study Results? - People with advanced cirrhosis. - People with HIV, hepatitis C or hepatitis D co-infection. - People with HBsAg levels above 3,000 IU/mL. Pharma Biotech FDA Clinical Trials Deals Drug Pricing Gene Therapy An article from GSK, Ionis win US approval for first-of-its-kind hepatitis B drug Hibsago is viewed as a potential “functional cure” for chronic infections and an important part of the British drugmaker’s goal of reaching £40 billion in annual revenue by 2031. Published Oct. 21, 2026 Delilah Alvarado Reporter Share Copy link Email LinkedIn X/Twitter Facebook Print License Add us on Google The U.S. Food and Drug Administration headquarters in Silver Spring, Md., on Nov. 10, 2020. Alamy The Food and Drug Administration has approved a first-of-its-kind medicine from GSK and Ionis Pharmaceuticals that’s been hailed as a possible “functional cure” for persistent hepatitis B infections. U.S. regulators cleared that therapy, known as Hibsago, on Tuesday for use alongside standard antiviral therapies in certain adults who have chronic hepatitis B infections but haven’t developed cirrhosis. Use is recommended specifically for people who’ve been on antivirals for at least six months, have suppressed levels of hepatitis B virus in their blood and low counts of a protein indicating they have an active infection. Treatment is given via periodic injections over the course of six months. All but the first can be self-administered, according to GSK. GSK didn’t disclose the drug’s list price. It’ll be revealed following the “completion of pricing and reimbursement discussions with payers,” a company spokesperson wrote in an email to BioPharma Dive. The hepatitis B virus is commonly transmitted from mother to child during birth. Infections can be prevented by vaccination, but when they aren’t, they can become chronic and eventually cause major health problems such as cirrhosis and liver cancer. GSK estimates these festering infections affect 1.7 million people in the U.S. and 240 million worldwide. Patients with chronic hepatitis B typically rely on lifelong antiviral therapy to suppress the virus. Hibsago, though, works differently. It’s an RNA-based medicine that both stops the virus’ ability to replicate and spurs an immune response. That mechanism is supposed to help the therapy more effectively clear infections, providing patients with the chance at a “functional cure,” or undetectable levels of the virus and its related proteins for at least 24 weeks. In the two late-stage studies supporting the drug’s approval, a combination of Hibsago and antivirals effectively wiped out the virus in about a fifth of recipients, compared to none who received placebo with antivirals. The results were published in the New England Journal of Medicine and hailed by analysts as a “landmark moment” in care for the condition. “Despite current therapies, many people living with chronic hepatitis B remain on treatment indefinitely and continue to face the risk of serious liver complications. For the first time, U.S. patients have the potential to achieve functional cure after a six-month treatment course,” Tony Wood, GSK’s chief scientific officer, said in a statement. In a note to clients Wednesday, Jefferies analyst Michael Leuchten wrote that the FDA’s prescribing information supports his firm’s expectations of around $3 billion in peak annual sales. The FDA’s labeling did, however, come with a safety warning for sudden spikes in liver inflammation or enzyme levels as well as low platelet counts. The agency recommended that patients get weekly or bi-weekly lab tests to check for those side effects, requirements that might “work against the commercial uptake” and slow adoption outside of specialty centers, Leuchten wrote. Still, the approval could bring GSK closer to achieving its goal of reaching £40 billion in annual revenues by 2031. Hibsago is one of many drugs featured in the drugmaker’s “accelerate growth” plan to offset key patent expirations. Hibsago has already been approved in Japan and is under regulatory reviews in China and Europe. Kennedy Jr. joins U.S. President Donald Trump as he signs an executive order calling for childhood vaccine shots to be spaced out into separate visits during an event in the Oval Office of the White House on August 10, 2026, in Washington, DC. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images A new modeling study projects that delaying or omitting the hepatitis B birth dose could increase chronic infections among children by 83% to 225%, depending on vaccine uptake rates. The CDC ended its universal recommendation for hepatitis B vaccination at birth in late 2025, shifting to individual-based decision making for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Up to 90% of infants infected with hepatitis B during their first year develop chronic infection, which can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer. The American Academy of Pediatrics still recommends universal vaccination within 24 hours of birth. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s proposed changes to the childhood vaccine schedule have raised alarm among public health experts and researchers. Concerns include a rise in preventable infectious diseases such as measles, polio, and hepatitis B. A new study suggests that delaying or foregoing the hepatitis B shot for newborns could increase chronic infections among children. In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) ended its recommendation for universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for the virus. Instead, the federal health agency recommendsTrusted Source individual-based clinical decision making. After reviewing the evidence, the CDC, which is overseen by the HHS, concluded that newborns “face little risk of contracting hepatitis,” which deemed the vaccine, typically administered at birth, unnecessary. Experts say this shift in public health policy wasn’t based on science, and researchers warn of rising infection rates. “Hepatitis B immunizations have been proven to protect individuals against a serious and significant disease,” said Graham Tse, MD, pediatrician and chief medical officer of MemorialCare Miller Children’s & Women’s Hospital in Long Beach, CA. “The hepatitis B vaccines have several decades of history and have been proven safe and effective,” Tse said. “There has been no new data or evidence presented or uncovered to support delaying the newborn dose of hepatitis B.” Here’s what parents should know about making informed decisions with their child’s healthcare team. Delaying hepatitis B shot may raise infection risk by 83% A U.S. modeling study published in Annals of Internal Medicine on October 20 projected that delaying the first vaccine dose until 2 months could increase chronic hepatitis B infections among infants by 19% under one scenario. With shared decision making and lower vaccine uptake, projected increases ranged from 83% to 225%, compared with universal birth-dose vaccination. The researchers also estimated that up to 1.8 million young adults could remain susceptible to hepatitis B by age 20 under shared decision making, compared with 232,000 under universal birth dosing. Another study published in JAMA PediatricsTrusted Source in late April projected hundreds of additional chronic infections annually if the hepatitis B birth dose were delayed or omitted. However, these figures are model-based projections, rather than verified outcomes. Actual results will depend on vaccination rates and other factors. Clinics 5 miles away (95% of the U.S.) GET TESTED HSA/FSA Payments Accepted Walk-ins Welcome 4.8 ★'s on App Store What changed in the hepatitis B vaccine schedule? In December 2025, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) adopted a recommendationTrusted Source shifting away from universal hepatitis B vaccination at birth for infants whose mothers test negative for hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg). Under the new approach, parents and healthcare professionals can decide together whether to give the first dose at birth or defer it until the baby is 2 months old. The change followed an 8 to 3 vote by the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP), marking a departure from longstanding U.S. guidance. However, infants born to mothers who test positive for hepatitis B or whose infection status is unknown should still receive the hepatitis B vaccine and hepatitis B immune globulin (HBIG) within 12 hours of birth, according to the updated guidelines. Why is hepatitis B dangerous for infants? Hepatitis B is a viral infection that affects the liver. Although some infections resolve, newborns and infants face a higher risk of developing lifelong hepatitis B infection compared with adults. Up to 90% of infants infected during their first year develop chronic hepatitis B. “We have actual world evidence that vaccinating newborns for hepatitis B prevents hepatitis B infections later in life and the serious complications of that disease,” Tse said. Over time, chronic infection can lead to cirrhosis, liver failure, or liver cancer. “The danger of delaying the newborn hepatitis B shot is that individuals do not get vaccinated and thereby do not have protection against hepatitis B,” Tse said. Early vaccination helps protect young infants before potential exposure occurs, including situations in which maternal screening misses an infection. “Newborns can be infected with hepatitis B from a mother who is not aware they have a hepatitis B infection or from exposure later in life,” Tse said. “The risk is developing a hepatitis B infection, which can potentially lead to liver cancer, fulminant hepatitis, or severe end-stage liver disease.” What should parents know about vaccine safety? In contrast to the CDC, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) still recommends a universal hepatitis B vaccine dose within 24 hours of birth, followed by additional doses during infancy. The leading pediatric medical organization has raised concerns about the potential consequences of reduced vaccination rates. The hepatitis B vaccine has decades of safety and effectiveness data. Tse said the AAP’s vaccine schedule and recommendations are based on decades of study, use, and expert input, and provide the best protection against vaccine-preventable diseases. Parents who have questions about potential side effects, timing, or their baby’s individual risk should discuss them with a qualified healthcare professional. “Parents are confused, given the recommendations from CDC, HHS, and Kennedy differ from established and respected groups such as the American Academy of Pediatrics, the Infectious Disease Society of America, and several states,” Tse said. “Parents desire to keep their children safe, and having differing opinions and confusion will lead to reduced vaccination rates as parents experience doubt as to whom to listen to or believe.” Should your newborn get vaccinated against hepatitis B? While the updated CDC policy offers more flexibility for some families, lower vaccination uptake could lead to an increase in chronic hepatitis B infections. Ask your pediatrician about the benefits of vaccination against hepatitis B at birth, the risks of delaying the first dose, and the recommended schedule for completing the series. You can also ask how maternal screening results affect your baby’s protection. An informed conversation with your healthcare professional can help you weigh the evidence and choose a vaccination plan for your baby. “I see no argument whatsoever for changing the established vaccination schedule for hepatitis B,” Tse said. “There have been no new studies, no data, nor evidence to justify Kennedy’s proposed changes to the childhood immunization schedule. Delaying vaccinations or skipping vaccinations puts your child at risk for serious and significant diseases, which are all preventable,” Tse said. Advertisement Before starting chemotherapy, immunotherapy or another cancer treatment, many patients are asked to take a blood test for hepatitis B. During Liver Cancer Awareness Month in October, here is what to know about why that test matters, based on guidance from the American Society of Clinical Oncology (ASCO), published in July 2020, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), published in March 2023. Hepatitis B is a virus that infects the liver. Many people who have it do not know. The CDC estimates that 580,000 to 2.4 million people in the United States are living with hepatitis B infection, and that about two-thirds of them might be unaware they are infected. Why Hepatitis B Matters During Cancer Treatment In someone who has hepatitis B now, or who had it in the past, the virus can stay quiet in the body for years. Some cancer treatments weaken the immune system, which can allow the virus to become active again. This is called hepatitis B reactivation, and it can cause liver inflammation and liver damage. The CDC says people who have weakened immune systems should be considered at risk for reactivation. Knowing your hepatitis B status before treatment starts gives your care team the chance to prevent reactivation or catch it early. Who Should Get Tested for Hepatitis B People with cancer: ASCO recommends universal hepatitis B screening for patients with cancer who expect to receive systemic anticancer therapy, meaning treatment that travels through the body, such as chemotherapy, targeted therapy or immunotherapy. All adults: Separately, the CDC recommends that all adults ages 18 and older be screened for hepatitis B at least once in their lifetime. The CDC also notes that screening might be recommended for people starting cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy. Which Hepatitis B Tests Are Used Both ASCO and the CDC recommend three blood tests, often called a “triple panel,” to assess hepatitis B status. The hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) test can indicate a current infection, while the total hepatitis B core antibody (anti-HBc) test indicates a past or current infection. The hepatitis B surface antibody (anti-HBs) test shows whether a person has protection from vaccination or a past infection. According to ASCO, a negative anti-HBs result may indicate a higher risk of hepatitis B reactivation in people with a past infection.Both ASCO and the CDC point to the same three blood tests, often called a "triple panel": What Happens if Your Test Is Positive A positive hepatitis B test does not usually mean you cannot get cancer treatment. It means your care team will plan for it. According to ASCO's guidance: Antiviral medicine: Most people with a current infection (HBsAg-positive) should take an antiviral medicine to prevent reactivation. Some people with a past infection (HBsAg-negative and anti-HBc-positive) should also take one if their cancer treatment carries a significant risk of reactivation. Preferred medicines are entecavir, tenofovir disoproxil fumarate or tenofovir alafenamide. How long: Antiviral medicine is usually taken during cancer treatment and for up to 12 months afterward. Higher-risk treatments: ASCO names anti-CD20 antibodies, a type of treatment used for some lymphomas and leukemias, and stem cell transplants as treatments that may raise the risk of reactivation. Hormone therapy alone is not known to substantially raise the risk. Monitoring: Your care team may check blood levels of the virus (HBV DNA) and liver tests during and after treatment. People with a past infection who are not on high-risk treatment may be monitored closely and started on antiviral medicine at the first sign of reactivation. A liver specialist: ASCO recommends involving a clinician experienced in treating hepatitis B. What It Means for You A hepatitis B test is a simple blood draw that can protect your liver during cancer treatment. If you have never been tested, or are not sure, it is reasonable to ask before treatment begins. If you test positive, ask your team to explain your plan, including how long to take antiviral medicine and why it is important not to stop it on your own. Hepatitis infections often go unrecognized in people with cancer, as CURE has reported. For more news on cancer updates, research and education, don't forget to subscribe to CURE®'s newsletters here. Drug MT Newswires Thu, October 22, 2026 at 8:10 AM EDT 1 min read ABUS Arbutus Biopharma (ABUS) said Thursday the US Food and Drug Administration lifted a clinical hold on its AB-101 treatment for hepatitis B, letting the company run further trials of the drug in the country. AB-101 is a pill designed to switch on the body's immune response against the hepatitis B virus by blocking a protein called PD-L1, the company said. In a phase 1a/1b study, the drug was generally well tolerated, with strong target binding in seven chronic hepatitis B patients and a drop in virus surface protein in two patients at the 30 milligram dose, Arbutus said. Shares of the company were up 2.4% in Thursday premarket activity. supplementary_news.content: News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Insights Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event SUBSCRIBE Menu SUBSCRIBE Show Search News Drug Development FDA Manufacturing Deals Business Job Trends Cell and Gene Therapy Cancer Opinions Press Releases All News & Releases Podcasts Events Insights Jobs Companies Hotbeds More Reports Career Advice NextGen: Top Startups to Watch 40 Under 40 Best Places to Work Employer Resources Advertise Advertise Talent Solutions Post Jobs Submit a Press Release Submit an Event Search Query Submit Search News FDA GSK, Ionis win FDA nod for hepatitis B functional cure that controls virus after treatment October 21, 2026 | 3 min read | Tristan Manalac Twitter LinkedIn Facebook Email Print iStock, happy_lark Hibsago’s approval—a functional cure for certain patients with a hepatitis B infection—further validates Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ antisense platform, which has already generated two other new drug approvals this year. The FDA has given the go-ahead to GSK and Ionis Pharmaceuticals’ antisense oligonucleotide bepirovirsen for the treatment of chronic hepatitis B virus infection, giving some patients the chance to potentially get off long-term medication. Bepiroversen, to be marketed under the brand name Hibsago, can help patients achieve undetectable levels of the virus in the blood after six months—serving as a functional cure, according to GSK’s announcement on Tuesday. GSK has forecasted peak worldwide sales of over £2 billion ($2.67 billion) for the drug, Reuters reported in May. BMO Capital Markets was more conservative in their estimate, projecting peak risk-unadjusted sales of $659 million in a Tuesday afternoon investor note. Ionis will receive 10–12% tiered royalties on GSK’s sales—about $163 million, by BMO’s estimate—a “relatively modest” contribution to the company’s commercial business, the analysts wrote. But the approval “adds meaningful validation” of Ionis’ antisense oligonucleotide (ASO) platform after recent setbacks to the overall class, BMO continued. The firm pointed to the Phase 3 failure of Ionis’ AstraZeneca-partnered ASO Wainua in transthyretin-mediated amyloid cardiomyopathy (ATTR-CM) this summer and the September miss of Ultragenyx’s investigational ASO in Angelman syndrome. Rare diseases Ionis Paves Its Own Path as Initial Tryngolza Launch Defies Expectations Long an R&D company that partnered off assets, RNAi biotech Ionis Pharmaceuticals shifted in 2025 to bring two medicines to market alone. Analysts are already impressed—and there’s more to come in 2026. February 18, 2026 · 3 min read · Annalee Armstrong Read more Hibsago marks Ionis’ third ASO approval this year, following the September victory of Zanvastro for Alexander disease and the June clearance of Tryngolza to lower blood lipid levels and pancreatitis risk in patients with severe hypertriglyceridemia. “While [Hibsago’s] approval was generally anticipated, we view this as another indication of the capabilities for the ASO platform Ionis has built,” BMO wrote. Hibsago is given via subcutaneous injection every six months, and patients have the option to self-administer the drug after the first dose. It is indicated for use in combination with nucleos(t)ide analog reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTI) and is approved for adult patients who have no liver scarring, according to GSK. Patients must have also been on NRTI treatment for at least six months and meet certain biomarker thresholds, as determined by an FDA-approved test. Alongside Hibsago’s approval, the agency cleared Roche’s Elecsys HBsAg II quant II RxDx assay as a diagnostic device to identify patients with chronic hepatitis B who are eligible for treatment. The assay is also meant to help monitor patients while undergoing treatment. Originally developed by Ionis, Hibsago was licensed by GSK in August 2019 with $25 million upfront plus up to $262 million in milestones. The antisense therapy targets the genetic material of the hepatitis B virus and tags it for destruction. This mechanism prevents the virus’ replication, while also boosting the immune system’s capabilities to fight off the infection. The FDA previously granted Hibsago breakthrough and priority review designations. Hibsago’s approval was supported by data from the Phase 3 B-Well studies. The program consists of two late-stage studies, B-Well 1 and B-Well 2, which together enrolled more than 1,800 adults with chronic hepatitis B who had been exposed to NRTI treatment. Participants were given either Hibsago or placebo. Both trials primarily assessed for functional cure, defined as having no detectable levels of the virus for 24 weeks after ending all hepatitis B medication. Infectious disease GSK, Ionis’ hepatitis B functional cure effectively eliminates virus in nearly 20% of patients The antisense oligonucleotide was even more effective in patients with relatively low viral activity. More than one-quarter of these individuals had undetectable levels of the virus in the blood for at least six months after stopping treatment. May 28, 2026 · 2 min read · Tristan Manalac Read more Detailed findings from the B-Well studies presented in May showed that Hibsago resulted in a 19% functional cure response rate. None of the patients on placebo hit functional cure. In a key secondary analysis, GSK focused on patients with low baseline levels of the virus’ surface antigen. Hibsago treatment elicited a 26% functional cure rate in this subgroup, the pharma said on Tuesday. “Hibsago provides a new treatment approach that gives some patients the possibility of maintaining control of the virus after all chronic HBV treatment has ended,” Wendy Carter, acting director of the FDA’s Office of Infectious Diseases under the Center for Drugs of Evaluation and Research, said in an agency release. “This approval represents an important advance for people living with this serious disease.” As for safety, the FDA added a boxed warning on the Hibsago logo warning of serious liver reactions and low platelet counts, which the regulator said could aggravate the likelihood of potentially life-threatening bleeding. Other warnings for the drug include serious inflammatory side effects and declining kidney function. supplementary_news.content: HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER Monday, October 19, 2026 No Result View All Result Login HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER HOME NEWS EXPLORE CAREER Companies Jobs Lecturer PhD Studentship Postdoc Research Assistant EVENTS iGEM News Team PHOTOS VIDEO WIKI BLOG COMMUNITY FACEBOOK INSTAGRAM TWITTER No Result View All Result No Result View All Result Home NEWS Science News Health Simple Blood Ratios Outperform Standard Scores for Spotting Cirrhosis in Suppressed Hepatitis B by October 19, 2026 in Health Reading Time: 5 mins read 0 Simple Blood Ratios Outperform Standard Scores for Spotting Cirrhosis in Suppressed Hepatitis B Share on FacebookShare on TwitterShare on LinkedinShare on RedditShare on Telegram Patients with chronic hepatitis B whose viral DNA has been driven below the detection limit by antiviral therapy are often assumed to be in a quiescent phase of infection. Yet a growing body of evidence shows that hepatitis B virus RNA can remain detectable in their serum, signaling that the viral transcriptional machinery inside infected liver cells is still running. A new study published in Frontiers in Medicine suggests that in this HBV DNA-negative, HBV RNA-positive population, two inexpensive blood-derived indices—the Prognostic Nutritional Index (PNI) and the monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR)—can identify which patients have already progressed to cirrhosis, and that they do so better than the fibrosis scores clinicians routinely rely on. The research, conducted by Minying Li, Yan Fang, Yuhong Han, Tuantuan Li, Yan Liu, and Lichang Chen of the Department of Clinical Laboratory at the Second People’s Hospital of Fuyang City in China, enrolled 183 patients with chronic hepatitis B between March 2024 and March 2025. All participants had serum HBV DNA below 10 IU/mL, the detection limit of the quantitative PCR assay used, but HBV RNA at or above 100 copies/mL, the positivity threshold of a capture-probe-based RNA assay. Of these, 87 patients who had developed cirrhosis formed the observation group, while 96 patients without cirrhosis served as controls. All patients were on antiviral therapy, and laboratory measurements were collected after treatment. The diagnosis of cirrhosis was not based on liver biopsy, which was not routinely performed because of its invasive nature. Instead, the reference standard combined liver stiffness measurement by transient elastography—defined as 12.0 kilopascals or higher—with ultrasonographic features such as a nodular liver surface, blunt liver edge, and splenomegaly, and/or clinical signs of portal hypertension including platelet counts below 100 × 109/L or imaging-confirmed varices. Where biopsy results were available, they were prioritized and showed good concordance with the non-invasive criteria. Patients co-infected with other hepatitis viruses, those with malignancy, autoimmune liver disease, or severe cardiovascular, renal, or hematopoietic disease were excluded to keep the comparison clean. PNI is a composite score first proposed by Buzby and colleagues in 1980 for perioperative risk assessment. It is calculated as ten times the serum albumin concentration in grams per deciliter plus 0.005 times the total lymphocyte count, and it captures the intertwined status of nutrition and cellular immunity. MLR, by contrast, is simply the monocyte count divided by the lymphocyte count, and it reflects the balance between innate and adaptive immune activity. Both indices can be derived from a standard complete blood count and a routine biochemistry panel, making them far cheaper and more accessible than molecular assays or elastography. The comparison between groups revealed a coherent biological pattern. Cirrhotic patients had significantly lower white blood cell, lymphocyte, and monocyte counts, along with reduced total protein, albumin, and prealbumin, while aspartate aminotransferase (AST) and gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) were significantly higher. Notably, the mean and median values of most of these individual parameters remained within normal reference ranges in both groups, which is precisely why the composite indices mattered. PNI was significantly lower in the cirrhosis group (52.44 versus 57.10), and MLR was significantly higher (0.21 versus 0.16), with both differences highly significant. Importantly, age, sex, ALT, ALP, and alpha-fetoprotein levels did not differ between groups, establishing baseline comparability. Diagnostic performance was assessed with receiver operating characteristic analysis. PNI achieved an area under the curve of 0.821 with a sensitivity of 95.8 percent at a cut-off of 53.15, while MLR reached an AUC of 0.743 with a sensitivity of 85.4 percent at a cut-off of 0.195. Strikingly, the established fibrosis scores FIB-4 and APRI managed only AUCs of 0.733 and 0.735, respectively, in the same cohort. The authors attribute this shortfall to the fact that FIB-4 and APRI depend heavily on transaminase and platelet dynamics, which tend to normalize when HBV DNA is suppressed, whereas PNI and MLR capture the nutritional-immune axis and systemic inflammation that continue to shift as cirrhosis develops. Within the cirrhosis group, PNI and MLR were also inversely correlated (r = −0.484, P < 0.001), underscoring that the two markers probe related but distinct facets of the same process. Multivariable logistic regression, with backward stepwise elimination guided by the Akaike Information Criterion and multicollinearity screened using variance inflation factors, confirmed that both indices were independent predictors. Higher PNI behaved as a protective factor, with an odds ratio of 0.694 per unit increase, while elevated MLR was a risk factor with an odds ratio of 3.176. Because MLR showed a markedly right-skewed distribution that destabilized continuous modeling, the team dichotomized it at the optimal ROC-derived cut-off for screening. From these independent predictors the researchers built a nomogram—a graphical scoring tool that translates individual biomarker values into a personalized probability of cirrhosis. The model achieved a concordance index of 0.829, and calibration curves showed good agreement between predicted and observed probabilities, while decision curve analysis indicated positive net clinical benefit. The mechanistic story the authors propose is subtle and hinges on the difference between HBV DNA and HBV RNA as virological markers. HBV DNA largely reflects active virion production and correlates with overt cytopathic injury, driving the transaminase spikes and platelet changes that FIB-4 and APRI were designed to detect. Persistent serum HBV RNA, particularly pregenomic RNA, instead signals ongoing transcription from the nuclear cccDNA reservoir—the stable minichromosome that nucleos(t)ide analogues cannot eradicate and the fundamental reason hepatitis B is difficult to cure and prone to relapse after treatment withdrawal. In this DNA-suppressed but RNA-positive state, the inflammatory pattern shifts from cytopathic to a chronic, smoldering, immune-mediated process. Viral RNA acts as a pathogen-associated molecular pattern recognized by Toll-like receptors on monocytes and Kupffer cells, sustaining innate activation and relative lymphopenia, while chronic low-grade inflammation suppresses hepatic albumin synthesis as a negative acute-phase reactant. These shifts preferentially perturb the immuno-nutritional axis that PNI and MLR measure. The study’s limitations are candidly acknowledged. The retrospective, cross-sectional, single-center design means the findings demonstrate association rather than causation or temporal prediction. The specificity of both biomarkers was modest—56.3 percent for PNI and 57.5 percent for MLR—so false positives are a real risk and the markers should be interpreted alongside imaging and other clinical parameters rather than as standalone tests. The nomogram has not yet been externally validated, and incomplete medical records prevented reliable accounting of antiviral regimens, treatment durations, HBeAg status, and HBV RNA levels, leaving room for residual confounding. The authors call for multicenter prospective studies and suggest exploring whether nutritional interventions guided by these biomarkers could improve outcomes. Even with those caveats, the practical appeal is considerable. Unlike HBV RNA or quantitative HBsAg testing, which require specialized molecular platforms that may be unavailable in resource-limited settings, PNI and MLR can be calculated from laboratory data that virtually every hospital already generates. The Fuyang team’s work suggests that in the growing population of patients whose HBV DNA has been silenced but whose cccDNA quietly persists, the most informative signals of advancing liver disease may lie not in viral load measurements but in the humble complete blood count and albumin value—indices that cost almost nothing and are already sitting in the medical record.
